Sports.title: The long-awaited return of Carlos Alcaraz, Alexandra Eala mania... and can Arthur Fery repeat his Wimbledon heroics? What we're excited about ahead of the US Open in New York
Sports.content:
The final slam of the tennis calendar at the US Open is just around the corner - and it could be the most unpredictable major of the season.

The ATP and WTA have been a Ferris wheel of injuries, with several top stars doubtful to compete, blowing both draws wide open. Anything could happen.

So, ahead of the action getting underway, Daily Mail Sport has picked out five reasons to get excited for the fortnight coming up at Flushing Meadows.

Carlos Alcaraz's comeback

Carlos Alcaraz confirmed his long-awaited return last Thursday in a collaboration post with football transfer journalist Fabrizio Romano, using his iconic 'Here we go' catchphrase.

After missing both Roland Garros and Wimbledon with an ongoing wrist injury, his round-one match in New York will be his first competitive singles outing since the Barcelona Open four months ago.

His withdrawal from the Cincinnati Open, where he was expected to make a comeback, leaves real questions over whether he can suddenly cope with the physical demands of five-set matches.

Carlos Alcaraz is set to be back in action at the US Open after a lengthy period out injured

World No 1 Jannik Sinner has pulled out though, leaving the tournament wide open

His long-standing rival Jannik Sinner has confirmed he will miss the US Open. The world No 1 hasn't played a competitive match since the Wimbledon final, nursing what has now been revealed as a right knee injury.

Aside from his dramatic second-round exit at Roland Garros, Sinner has been ruthless for large parts of the season. He defended his Wimbledon title with ease and became the second man after Rafael Nadal to win all three Clay Court Masters 1000 events in a single year.

A Grand Slam without Sinner or Alcaraz as the favourite is a foreign concept – they’ve won nine of the last ten majors between them.

With Sinner out and Alcaraz back after a long absence, the chasing pack have a rare chance to shine under the Arthur Ashe lights.

Star-studded mixed doubles return

The revamped mixed doubles format returns following its controversial introduction last year. With shorter sets, a substantial cash prize and a slot a week before the singles draw, it is designed to lure the top singles stars into competing.

After much speculation, Alcaraz and Serena Williams have confirmed they will join forces. The blockbuster pairing - with a combined 44 singles and double Grand Slam - have received a wildcard into the main draw.

Defending champions Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori will chase a third straight title and reiterate to the organisers that doubles specialists shouldn’t be undermined or disposable.

Other partners include 24-time-Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic and world No 1 Aryna Sabalenka, all-American duo Jessica Pegula and Taylor Fritz, plus wildcard partnerships such as spouses Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils, and Russian pair Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev.

Following qualifiers this week, Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool, as well as Katerina Siniakova and Brit Henry Patten, advanced to the main draw, which begins on Tuesday with the semi-finals and final scheduled for tomorrow.

Several star-studded pairs are set to play together in the mixed doubles event, including Novak Djokovic (above) and women's world No 1 Aryna Sabalenka

Alexandra Eala mania

If one thing is for certain, count on Alexandra Eala’s electric Filipino fanbase to flood Flushing Meadows.

Her meteoric rise to stardom has launched the Philippines into a tennis-obsessed nation. The 21-year-old’s influence has pushed local governments to build thousands of more hardcourts across the country.

Eala arrives in the form of her life, fresh off her biggest career title at the Washington Open – triumphing against world number five Jessica Pegula in the final.

The left-handed youngster also had a standout grass court swing: winning a WTA 250 event in Birmingham, reaching the semi-final of the Berlin Open and then at Wimbledon, she beat defending champion Iga Swiatek in straight sets in the third round.

Expect lots of Filipino flags, enthusiastic chants in Tagalog and a player riding a wave of national pride.

Alexandra Eala’s electric Filipino fanbase are set to flood Flushing Meadows to cheer her on

Can Fery go again?

Before Wimbledon, Arthur Fery was seldom mentioned as a serious British prospect, having gone about his business quietly on the ITF and ATP challenger circuit.

Now, the 24-year-old is ranked 37 in the world after a historic wildcard run to the semi-finals at the All-England club.

Fery, who grew up in Wimbledon, has played only one tournament since, reaching the second round in Cincinnati before falling to Alex De Minaur in two tight sets.

With Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu both withdrawing due to injury and Katie Boulter and Cameron Norrie rarely threatening at the business end of Slams, Brits will be hoping Fery’s unexpected rise is no fluke.

Arthur Fery had a fairytale run at Wimbledon so this will be another exciting challenge for him

The pursuit to be women’s world No 1

Aryna Sabalenka could be dethroned from the top of the WTA rankings in New York, with Elena Rybakina, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula all able to leapfrog her depending on results.

Sabalenka hasn’t reached a final since completing the Sunshine Double in March – a worrying dip by her standards. To retain the top spot, she must win the US Open outright.

Rybakina has shown a recent upturn in form, reaching the Canadian Open final and then the Cincinnati quarter-finals before an ankle injury cut her run short, putting her participation in doubt. If she plays, reaching the semi-finals would guarantee her world No 1 status.

Cincinnati champion Gauff and Cincinnati and Washington finalist Pegula can also climb to No 1 if they win the tournament and Rybakina loses before the semi-finals.

The women’s draw has no obvious frontrunner, and the title feels up for grabs. With four players mathematically in contention, the race for women's world No 1 remains one of the most compelling storylines heading into the US Open.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes 'needs to keep his mouth shut', says Man United legend Paul Scholes - as he also demands Harry Maguire explain bizarre 'hug' on team-mate before Hull goal
Sports.content:
Bruno Fernandes 'needs to keep his mouth shut', says Man United legend Paul Scholes - as he also demands Harry Maguire explain bizarre 'hug' on team-mate before Hull goal

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former Manchester United midfielder Paul Scholes has criticised Bruno Fernandes' post-match comments after United's opening-day loss to Hull at the weekend.

United fell to a 2-0 defeat at the MKM Stadium on Saturday, conceding both goals from set pieces in the first half of the opening Premier League weekend. Newly promoted Hull have been widely tipped as favourites for relegation.

After the match, the United captain complained to the media that his side had made the 'same mistakes as we did last season (in away matches)'. The Portugal midfielder added: 'Every away game we give too much of the ball to them. In the first 20 minutes, the goalkeeper was the one with the most touches.

'We needed to press more, be more aggressive, and then again we need to work on set plays and not concede these types of goals. Against these types of teams, they are waiting for that moment.'

Scholes, however, has taken issue with Fernandes' comments on his podcast The Good, The Bad & The Football, sponsored by Midnite.

'I'd be interested to know what he means by them. What mistakes were they giving away?' the 51-year-old former player said.

Scholes criticised Fernandes' complaints about his side's performance, saying: 'Especially when you perform the way he did as well, I think it's probably to keep your mouth shut'

The United captain had said after the defeat to Hull that his side had made the 'same mistakes as we did last season (in away matches)'

'Especially when you perform the way he did as well, I think it's probably best to keep your mouth shut. He didn't have his best performance either.'

Scholes and former United forward Dion Dublin went further, suggesting that Fernandes, alongside team-mate Luke Shaw, who also claimed after the match that United went into the fixture underprepared, had undermined manager Michael Carrick.

Shaw had said after the match: 'It’s not us and we knew it was coming. I think as a whole, as a group, collectively, we could prepare better. Especially knowing how good they are at set plays and what their dangers are.'

Reacting to the left-back's comments, Scholes said: 'Luke Shaw always says something. And that's a slight on your staff. That's a slight on your manager. If one of your players is saying that you'd be like f***ing hell, you'd have them in on Monday morning.'

Dublin said: 'You want silence. If your skipper has to speak then he has to speak, but then you make sure he says the things that don't open a can of worms. You just don't give anyone any ammunition because the ammunition is there from your performance.'

Scholes added: 'Those comments are not so much about respect but you speak about fear of managers and the things they've said, they're a slight on the manager and staff. As a player if we did that about Sir Alex, "we weren't prepared", f***ing hell, you'd be right in and he'd probably single you out in front of the full team.'

Dublin had preceded these comments by claiming that the 'hardest thing' for Carrick is that he has to 'sever' his close relationships with the players in order to stamp his authority.

'The friend or colleague issue that he had as an interim, the hardest thing now that he is permanent is that he is going to have to sever those connections, which I think will be hard for someone like Michael because he's a nice bloke.

Harry Maguire held onto Noussair Mazraoui as Hull City scored their first goal on Saturday

'But now he's the manager he's going to have to (stop) the "how are you doing pal", "how are you doing mate", "do you fancy going for a beer". You can't do that anymore. (Now, it's) I'm the manager, you're that. Do as you're told.'

Meanwhile, Scholes also reacted to Harry Maguire accidentally marking team-mate Noussair Mazraoui in the build-up to Hull's opening goal from a corner.

The centre-back had his arms around Mazraoui before the man he was supposed to be marking, Semi Ajayi, headed the ball into the net.

Scholes added: 'The only thing I can think is that he's lost his bearings. He's looking at the ball, he can feel somebody in front of him, and he's just gone like that (hugging motion).

'It doesn't look good, does it? I'd like to hear him explain it.'

United return to action on Sunday at home to another promoted side in Ipswich Town.

Sports.title: How the Owens fell in love with horse racing: former England star Michael and daughter Gemma take us on a tour of their luxurious Cheshire stables... as former Love Island star bids to make it as a professional jockey
Sports.content:
How the Owens fell in love with horse racing: former England star Michael and daughter Gemma take us on a tour of their luxurious Cheshire stables... as former Love Island star bids to make it as a professional jockey

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

At the start of the new documentary series which follows both his and his family's lives, Michael Owen is posed a question.

'You've got a bit of a reputation for being a…' the producer begins, before being cut off by the former striker mid-sentence.

'Boring p***k!' shouts the ex-Liverpool, Real Madrid, Newcastle and England striker. Owen is clearly aware of the perception some have of him as dull, but there can be no doubting the passion he has for his life in football retirement.

Owen's love for horse racing radiates out of his every pore as he and daughter Gemma show Daily Mail Sport around the family's luxurious Manor House Stables in rural Cheshire. 'It hasn't rained here for three months,' Owen says, huddling under an umbrella, but refusing to allow a rare, heavy rain shower to dampen his enthusiasm.

'This is my pride and joy. My little baby. I'm a geek. I know every horse, every owner and every race coming up. I could keep talking to you about horses for ages.'

At his peak, Owen terrorised opposition defenders with his pace and finishing which saw him become one of football's deadliest hitmen around. Now, his days are about speed of a different kind.

Racing consumes Owen, as football once did. His Love Island star daughter, 23, is bidding to become a professional jockey and continues to train as a dressage rider after she finished fourth in the Magnolia Cup – a charity flat race – at Glorious Goodwood earlier this summer. 'I've just fallen in love with the sport,' Gemma says. 'I don't want to give it up.'

Racing is also now a family affair for the Owen family, with daughter Gemma and dad Michael showing Daily Mail Sport around their luxurious Manor House Stables in rural Cheshire

Gemma is bidding to become a professional jockey and continues to train as a dressage rider

'I've just fallen in love with the sport,' Gemma says. 'I don't want to give it up'

Michael has owned Manor House Stables for more than 20 years and now runs the business with Hugo Palmer as trainer. He employs more than 50 people, looking after more than 130 horses. It is his pride and joy.

'It's the most stressful thing in the world, but I wake up every morning and I'm excited to come here,' Michael says. Racing is at the epicentre of Meet the Owens, a six-part Amazon series which has Michael and Gemma as leading lights.

Michael has an array of top current or former footballers as owners of horses at his yard, including England's new Barcelona ace Anthony Gordon, Tottenham's Andy Robertson, Paul Scholes, Steve McManaman and Owen Hargreaves among many others. Sir Alex Ferguson and the squad of Premier League side Brighton are also involved, as are darts stars Luke Littler and Stephen Bunting. The list goes on and on.

Michael ensures no stone is left unturned in his bid to achieve on-track success. He insists all of his horses are in stables with windows on either side, so their inquisitive nature can be satisfied.

A swimming pool aids horses with their recovery and on the day we visit, seven-year-old Box To Box - one of the oldest horses in the yard - is the one to take the plunge. Box To Box is named because it is owned by a consortium which includes former midfielders Hargreaves and McManaman.

It is noticeable as you tour Manor House how pristine the facility is. There are no piles of steaming horse manure. No stench. Nothing is too out of place, despite it being a working yard.

Franny Norton, a former jockey who won just under 2,000 races in a 36-year career, buzzes about - his scouse accent and colourful language lighting up the yard. Norton acts as a riding advisor to Michael and helped Gemma to get up to speed with what's needed to be a top jockey.

'James Milner is the luckiest owner ever. Everything he touches turns into a superstar!' says Michael, still only 46, as he shows off his incredible, top-of-the-range facility featuring equine swimming pool, electronic horse walker and even an ice bath.

Racing is also now a family affair for the Owen family, with Gemma looking to make her way in the sport. 'To be honest, it took me by surprise how much I have loved racing and learning a new skill,' says Gemma, who now works alongside her father's riders on a daily basis.

'I thought I would do the Magnolia Cup and it would be an amazing experience, but then that would be it. I've always had horses and gone to the races, but spending more time at Manor House with the staff has allowed me to connect with the sport on a deeper level. I'll continue and try and get my amateur jockey licence and then hopefully ride in a few more races.

Gemma says she has connected with the sport of horseracing 'on a deeper level' recently

Gemma dreams of winning a race - and her dad has been serious about the business for years

'Juggling racing and dressage has been difficult, but I want to try and continue the two. I've done dressage for as long as I can remember. Racing is completely different. It's definitely brought the family closer. It's nice that we share that passion.

'The dream would be to win a race. That's going to be the target.'

In 2022, Gemma starred on season eight of Love Island, finishing as a runner-up on the hit reality show. With 1.6million followers on Instagram, her love for racing as well as fashion – Gemma also runs a swimwear business – is a priceless opportunity for the sport to reach a younger audience at a time when it needs to do exactly that.

'Racing is trying to attract younger people,' Gemma says. 'It has a fashion element to it which does that. With my background in horses, Manor House and my interest in fashion, I'd like to be able to bring other people into racing. That doesn't mean they have to ride.

'I like to show my followers into the racing world.'

Michael's successful football career – he retired in 2013 after 40 goals in 89 England appearances and as the last English winner of the Ballon d'Or – has laid the platform for his multi-million-pound racing business as well as his family's luxurious life.

But he is not playing at racing. For him, it's more than serious.

He has had success too, saddling winners at the highest level of flat racing in England as well as across the world. 'If I get my teeth into something, I'm all in. It's just how I am,' Michael says.

'It was the same with football and now it's the same with racing. Everything you see here is the fruits of our labour. You can't help but have a soft spot for the people you employ, the horses you train, the owners you meet and the friends you make.

'I lasted in football till l I was 33, but I'd like to think this would be something I die doing.'

Managing, owning and buying and selling top flat horses – as well as the daily costs of running a yard – means Michael's Manor House Stables is a business of high costs and even higher stakes.

Like in football, only one thing matters – winning.

'I've got no qualms in saying it's become a family business and that means a lot,' he added. 'It brings you a little bit closer. It's been lovely and I can only see it continuing. Gemma is not stopping now she's got a taste for riding.

Managing, owning and buying and selling top flat horses means Michael's Manor House Stables is a business of high costs and even higher stakes

After years working in football, Michael is not playing at racing. For him, it's more than serious

'She's going to be competing as an amateur and God knows where it's going to take her. But she absolutely loves it. I didn't feel pressure as a footballer. It came naturally.

'I wouldn't use the word pressure to describe running this business, but I do have to think about how I want it to run. It's very different.' Michael has four children in total and his son James – who is now clinically blind due to a rare eye condition – is also involved at Manor House behind the scenes.

'There are so many women jockeys coming through the ranks. The likes of Hollie Doyle and Saffie Osborne are incredible role models. I look up to them and admire them for what they've done,' Gemma adds.

'I'm just trying to take it step by step. I'm still so new to the sport. You don't appreciate the strength jockeys need. I had to go through a lot of fitness tests to compete in the Magnolia Cup.

'That process was so hard. Jockeys are very, very strong. I've got a new-found respect for them. I would also love to do a Grand Prix on my dressage horse. I've not yet been able to compete at that level.

'My horse is very experienced and he's very talented. However, he is not a straightforward ride.

'I feel like I'm more involved with the family business now. It does feel more special. My brother takes an interest in the business side of things and my mum has become more involved as well.

'It's nice that it's brought us all together and I can share my passion for racing with my parents.'

All six episodes of Meet the Owens will be available to stream on Amazon Prime Video from August 28.

Sports.title: Why Chelsea's 'JPMorgan' front three have a huge advantage over title rivals after flying start at Fulham - and the clue that Mike Penders is creeping closer to starting place after Robert Sanchez howlers, writes KIERAN GILL
Sports.content:
Why Chelsea's 'JPMorgan' front three have a huge advantage over title rivals after flying start at Fulham - and the clue that Mike Penders is creeping closer to starting place after Robert Sanchez howlers, writes KIERAN GILL

Unlock more from Kieran Gill inside the Chelsea camp with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight, analysis and more

As Cole Palmer sat down with us at Chelsea's training base in Sydney, Australia, there was a whiteboard to his right-hand side with the WiFi password written on it: ‘F00tB4ll15C0mingH0m3!’

Palmer never made it to the World Cup with England, and football failed to come home under Thomas Tuchel, and so we discussed how he had spent his restful summer instead.

Palmer: ‘I had like seven weeks off. Which I've never really had. I feel fresh.’ Did you know what to do with yourself with all that time? Palmer: ‘Nah. It was strange. I didn’t know where to go. I got bored after like six weeks. I was sat in Marbella thinking, “I want to go back”.’ Did watching the World Cup give you greater hunger for next season? Palmer: ‘Naturally. It’s like anything. If someone told you that you're essentially not good enough to get in the squad, then you’re going to think alright, whatever, then try to go that extra harder.’

That he did at Craven Cottage. He twisted and turned Antonee Robinson until Fulham’s left back resembled a pretzel at times. Palmer brought the mustard even when Alvaro Arbeloa had Cesar Palacios or Alex Iwobi dropping deep to help out Robinson.

It appeared futile, because Palmer played like a man who had missed football, as if he could not wait to be back on that field. Recharged. Rebooted. Ready. He was not alone in that regard. Chelsea’s XI which opened the season with a 3-2 victory at Craven Cottage carried a collective total of 1,046 World Cup minutes in their legs.

By comparison, Manchester City’s XI had 3,351 minutes. Liverpool: 2,279. Arsenal: 2,191. Manchester United: 1,687. They are Chelsea’s primary rivals for finishing in the Champions League places – or higher.

Cole Palmer looks fit and firing after being snubbed by England head coach Thomas Tuchel for his World Cup squad over the summer

Palmer scored one and set up another to get Chelsea's Premier League campaign off to a flier at Fulham on Monday night

It's no wonder Chelsea's front three looked so fresh - Joao Pedro (left) and Palmer were not picked for the World Cup, while Morgan Rogers (right) started only three games for England

Chelsea's total will rise when Ecuador's Moises Caicedo returns from his minor setback, and depending if he stays, it would likewise be increased by Enzo Fernandez, the Argentina midfielder who was sent off in the World Cup final and was booed by Fulham fans as they chanted ‘England, England’ at Craven Cottage.

However, this could yet act as a weapon for Xabi Alonso this season alongside their lack of European football. Chelsea are fresher, focused, and have players with personal points to prove.

Palmer and his £117million best friend Morgan Rogers kickstarted their partnership against Fulham, while Joao Pedro, another excluded from the World Cup by Brazil, scored within 31 seconds. He is on nine goals from nine games under Alonso including their pre-season friendlies.

This attacking trident has already been blessed with a new nickname – 'J P Morgan' – and with a goal apiece, their account is up and running.

Sanchez out, Penders in?

A team is only as serious as the man they have in goal, and while Robert Sanchez is a fine goalkeeper, it remains debatable whether he can take Chelsea to the next level.

Both of Fulham’s goals were avoidable. Josh King scored from the edge of the area, but he had been encouraged to shoot from distance earlier on when Sanchez made an unconvincing save.

According to the Expected Goals (xG) statistic, a goalkeeper would be expected to save King’s equaliser 97 per cent of the time. Sanchez also parried a shot towards the head of Gonzalo Garcia for Fulham’s second goal.

In 2020, Kepa Arrizabalaga put in a poor performance at home to Liverpool, with Chelsea boss Frank Lampard describing the second goal in that 2-0 loss as a ‘clear mistake’. The club reacted by signing Edouard Mendy before that window's end.

A team is only as serious as the man they have in goal, and while Robert Sanchez is a fine goalkeeper, it remains debatable whether he can take Chelsea to the next level

Chelsea see enormous potential in Mike Penders, who spent last season on loan with Strasbourg, and he is expected to start the Carabao Cup tie against Luton on Thursday

Chelsea sources have spent all of this summer maintaining that they are happy with their goalkeeping setup. Entering this season, that was with Sanchez as No1 and Mike Penders as No2, and it was taken into consideration that any new arrival could block Penders’ pathway.

Chelsea see enormous potential in the 21-year-old Belgian, who spent last season on loan with Strasbourg, though he may not have to wait too long to get his chance to impress.

Unless Alonso decides he needs to give Sanchez the chance to boost his confidence after his mistakes made at Fulham, Penders is expected to start in their Carabao Cup clash this Thursday against League One Luton Town, who are managed by former Arsenal midfielder Jack Wilshere.

Alonso said at his first press conference of the season, when asked about his goalkeepers, that ‘the pitch is the boss of everything’. Alonso embraced Sanchez at full time after their win over Fulham, but from the outside, it is already looking like advantage Penders.

Sports.title: Outgrounds, grey water and digging up strips: How Lord's is fighting back against pitch crisis in brutal heat wave - and the problems facing every English county with '18 different answers'
Sports.content:
Outgrounds, grey water and digging up strips: How Lord's is fighting back against pitch crisis in brutal heat wave - and the problems facing every English county with '18 different answers'

Unlock more of the best of our cricket coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

There will be a sharp intake of breath when the second Test between England and Pakistan gets underway at Lord’s on Thursday morning.

Back in early June, the Test there against New Zealand began with a delivery from Matt Henry that kept low outside Ben Duckett’s off-stump and bounced twice on the way through to Jamie Smith.

Three days later, after England had won a low-scoring shootout in which three of the four innings failed to reach 150, MCC apologised for the inconsistency of the surface. Two days after that, the ICC labelled it ‘unsatisfactory’, and slapped Lord’s with an unprecedented demerit point.

The home of cricket scolded by the authorities? It was as if the parish vicar had been overheard using profanities in the vestibule.

‘It was a hard couple of days,’ says Rob Lynch, MCC’s director of cricket and operations. ‘It hurt. But we put our hands up straight away.’

Lynch, not unreasonably, calls the Lord’s pitch ‘the most scrutinised 22 yards in world sport’. But his acceptance that the surface for the New Zealand game wasn’t up to scratch might have been on behalf of the entire English game, with groundstaff everywhere struggling to combat a summer of heat waves and a fixture list that has mushroomed beyond all reason.

MCC had to apologise for the quality of the Lord's surface after England won a low-scoring shootout against New Zealand in June in which three of the four innings failed to reach 150

Jacob Bethell reacts after being bowled by a Matt Henry delivery that barely got above shin height

There are exceptions. Headingley received widespread praise for the pitch it produced for last week’s first Test, while The Oval has regularly provided the pace and bounce England craved under Brendon McCullum.

But a more typical response came last summer, after England had lost to India at Edgbaston. Ben Stokes had chosen to bowl first in the expectation of early assistance for his seamers, but instead watched the Indians rack up 587. He later complained: ‘It ended up being more of a subcontinent pitch.’

At stake, then, is not simply the question of home advantage, which England – traditionally the spiritual home of grey skies, green pitches, seam and swing – are in danger of ceding, but the ability of overworked groundstaff to come up with surfaces that simultaneously please players and pundits, spectators and executives.

Three major problems have fed English cricket’s pitch crisis. The first is sheer volume, with the advent of the Hundred and the growth of the women’s game adding to the workload. Of the 20 pitches on the Lord’s square, only seven can be used for televised games, and only five for major matches. Sooner or later, something has to give.

The second is county cricket’s centralisation. The outgrounds which once eased the pressure on county HQs play less of a role than they once did as clubs look to cut costs by focusing on their main venue.

Then there’s the drought, which has been good for spectators but a nightmare for groundstaff unsure how best to balance the traditional skills of watering and rolling pitches. Preparation at Lord’s for the New Zealand Test faced two extremes in quick succession during the build-up: a heat wave followed by torrential rain. The usual calculations went out of the window.

It was notable that July’s one-day international against India was preceded by calmer weather: Karl McDermott, the Lord’s head groundsman, produced a belter on which 747 runs were scored in 100 overs for the loss of ten wickets.

Trent Bridge, meanwhile, which staged the third Test of the New Zealand series, started so dry that cracks were visible beneath the early coating of grass. Two days before the game, McCullum was praying England won the toss. They did not – and went on to lose the series.

Bethell had better luck in the ODI at Lord's against India a month later, smashing 91 as part of England's mammoth 387 for three - in a match that produced more than 747 runs in 100 overs

Of the 20 pitches on the Lord’s square, only seven can be used for televised games, and only five for major matches. Sooner or later, something has to give

Perhaps the most sobering aspect of the Lord’s drama was that it was no great surprise. And what unfolded merely fortified Lynch’s belief that something had to be done. A seven-point action plan was drawn up, and MCC – as so often – are now at the forefront of tackling the problem.

They have brought in turf management experts, including Blair Christiansen, who is in charge of Auckland’s Eden Park but was also FIFA’s pitch manager for the World Cup final in New Jersey.

They are cultivating drop-in pitches, and hope to use one for an international match in 2029, and now use Wormsley – an hour’s drive from St John’s Wood up the M40 – to host around 35 days of cricket a year.

And they are making enhanced use of data to examine factors such as moisture levels, and will embark on a painstaking relaying process of some of the central pitches, starting by digging up the New Zealand strip, which takes it out of action for at least two years.

‘No two people were hurting more than Karl and me,’ says Lynch. ‘We feel the pressure. If we didn’t, we’d be in the wrong job.’

Some feel the ECB have allowed the matter to fester, and Neil Snowball, the board’s managing director of competitions and major events, admits the problem risks generating ‘18 different answers’ from each of the first-class counties.

But he says the ECB are planning to give host grounds between seven and nine clear days before each Ashes Test next summer to aid preparation, and are encouraging clubs to make greater use of their outgrounds, especially during the One-Day Cup, which clashes with the Hundred.

Snowball cites the example of Warwickshire, where he was previously chief executive and which this season staged three of its four one-day games at Rugby School rather than Edgbaston. And he wants to look at the number of non-professional matches staged by the major venues.

Middlesex have turned to using outgrounds for One-Day Cup matches, such as Radlett in Hertfordshire

Gloucestershire hosted a Championship match against Worcestershire at Cheltenham College this month

As for the UK’s ever hotter summers, water management is high on the agenda, with bore holes, underground storage and the use of ‘grey water’ (non-drinking water) all part of the discussion.

It’s a reminder that cricket is feeling its way through a subject that is less scientific than many critics of the Lord’s pitch appear to think.

And for all MCC’s good intentions, they will not breathe easily again until this week’s Pakistan Test goes by without too much scrutiny of those troublesome 22 yards.

Sports.title: Rugby league legend - and the sport's first knight - Sir Billy Boston dies ages 92
Sports.content:
Rugby league legend - and the sport's first knight - Sir Billy Boston dies ages 92

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Sir Billy Boston, who last year became the first rugby league player to be awarded a knighthood, has died at the age of 92.

The Welsh Rugby Union confirmed his death in a statement, saying: 'Sir Billy Boston, one of the best loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport, has passed away peacefully at the age of 92.

'The most famous son of Tiger Bay, he died overnight in hospital in his adopted home for the last 72 years, Wigan.

Today we mourn the loss of a true sporting icon, Sir Billy Boston, who has passed away surrounded by his family.



Rugby League’s first knight, a Wigan legend, and "Everybody's Hero," his legacy on and off the field will endure for eternity.



Rest in peace, Sir Billy. 🍒⚪️ pic.twitter.com/y8Dw9XPPGi — Wigan Warriors 🍒⚪️ (@WiganWarriorsRL) August 25, 2026

'His death came only four days after the funeral of his wife, Lady Joan, to whom he had been married for 70 years.'

Boston grew up playing rugby union before switching codes to sign for Wigan in 1953 at the age of 19. He went on to score 478 tries in 488 appearances for the club during the 1950s and 1960s.

Wigan head coach Matt Peet led the tributes to Boston, saying: ‘On behalf of myself, our coaching staff and players, from the first team through to our academy, we send our deepest condolences to Sir Billy’s family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly sad time.

'Billy Boston is woven into the fabric of this club. Every day we walk through the doors, we’re reminded that we have a responsibility to represent all those who have gone before us and made Wigan Warriors what is is today. Billy stands at the very top of that history.

'Those fortunate enough to have seen him play tell me he was simply the greatest. His achievements, the man he was and the standards he set will continue to inspire everyone who pulls on this shirt.

Sir Billy Boston was hailed as 'simply the greatest' by Wigan head coach Matt Peet

Boston was knighted by the King last year

'His legacy goes far beyond records and trophies. His impact on Wigan, on rugby league and on the wider sporting world was recognised at the very highest level. We will do everything we can to honour his memory by representing this club with the pride, humility and excellence that he embodied.

'Sir Billy Boston will always be one of Wigan Warriors’ greatest sons, and he will never be forgotten.'

Wigan have indicated that they will pay tribute to Boston prior to their Betfred Super League match against Hull KR on Thursday night.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

YouTube YouTube , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can use the buttons below to amend your preferences to enable YouTube cookies or to allow those cookies just once. In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Italy vs Northern Ireland

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina

Final: Wales/Bosnia and Herzegovina vs Italy/Northern Ireland - Tuesday, 7.45pm kick-off
