World.title: Hungary to reclaim EUR 303 million as government moves to scrap controversial foundations
World.content:
The ministry of science and technology will recover a total HUF 110 billion (EUR 303 million) through the elimination of public interest asset management foundations (KEKVA), Zoltán Tanács, the minister, said on Facebook on Monday.

Tanács said his portfolio would take over the activities of the ZalaZONE and Élvonal foundations, adding that while the “redundant” foundations would be scrapped, the ministry would maintain their activities. He also added that scrapping the system would save the ministry an annual HUF 800 million.

According to Tanács, the two foundations have a combined HUF 62.5 billion on their accounts, while they also have assets worth nearly HUF 50 billion. “That is over HUF 110 billion – from now on in public funds,” the minister added.

Tanács said both Élvonal’s and ZalaZONE’s activities were crucial, the first focusing on the development of young talents and building world-class scientific teams and the latter having an automotive research and development infrastructure, which could provide a test environment for self-driving cars, drones and robots in future. “But all that does not require an unnecessarily expensive, not sufficiently transparent or controlled foundation model,” he added.

World.title: Bucharest International Poetry Festival to take place in September
World.content:
The Bucharest International Poetry Festival (FIPB) is set to bring together poets and artists from around the world between September 14 and 20.

Organized by the Bucharest City Hall through the National Museum of Romanian Literature, this year’s festival proposes the theme “Slow Gun Poetry/Long-Range Poetry,” inspired by poet Cezar Ivănescu’s reflection on the power of a simple sign on a sheet of paper.

According to the organizers, the theme starts from the idea that from a word, ideas, consciences and even revolutions can be born, and that the true strength of the world does not lie in force, but in meaning.

“Poetry is not a form of escape from reality, but one of the most powerful ways of understanding it. At a time when words are increasingly used to separate, radicalize and build walls between people, the Bucharest International Poetry Festival assumes, through this edition, the mission of bringing the word back to its natural space: that of dialogue, freedom, empathy and the meeting between people and cultures,” said Ioan Cristescu, general director of the National Museum of Romanian Literature, cited in the press release.

This year’s edition features guests from the Republic of Armenia, Austria, the Czech Republic, Cyprus, China, Croatia, France, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, the Republic of Moldova, Peru, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Tunisia and Turkey, alongside numerous Romanian poets and artists. More than 50 events are included in the festival program: public readings, debates, conferences, exhibitions, concerts, performances, recitals and commemorative events.

The festival will officially open on Monday, September 14, at 18:00, in the Hall of the “Carol I” Central University Library. The opening ceremony will bring together representatives of partner cultural and diplomatic institutions, as well as ambassadors and representatives of cultural institutes from participating countries.

The evening will continue with a concert performed by the ARCO Chamber Ensemble, public readings by Romanian and international poets, and a reading-performance by Slovenian poet Aleš Šteger, recognized as one of the most original and translated voices in contemporary European literature, accompanied on accordion by Tori Jure.

An important component of this year’s edition of FIPB is dedicated to the memory and recovery of great Romanian poets. The program includes commemorative events dedicated to Cezar Ivănescu, Emil Botta, Constanța Buzea, Angela Marinescu, Marin Sorescu and Magda Isanos, organized in partnership with the Bucharest National Theatre. At the same time, this year’s edition marks 130 years since the birth of Tristan Tzara, founder of the Dada movement, through a workshop dedicated to children and adults, in which poetry meets visual art and calligrams.

Moreover, FIPB will feature programs dedicated to children and teenagers, such as comic book workshops, creative activities, literary games and numerous other projects.

World.title: Romania’s football team to face off against Sweden in Nations League match next month
World.content:
Romania’s national football team is set to play against Sweden on Friday, September 25, within League B of the Nations League. The match will be played in Solna, Sweden, according to an announcement on the official FRF website.

Starting Tuesday, August 25, and until Friday, September 18 (or until they run out), tickets for the game against Sweden will be available on the FRF website. The price of a ticket, set by the organizers of the match, is RON 130, with 2,200 seats in the stadium’s North Stand (sectors 116-121) allocated to the Romanian fans. Each supporter can order a maximum of 4 tickets before completing an order, and the tickets will be nominative.

Group B4 of the Nations League also includes Bosnia-Herzegovina and Poland. After the match with Sweden, the Romanian team will face Bosnia-Herzegovina on September 28, then Poland on October 2.

Rematches will take place on October 5 against Sweden, November 14 against Poland, and November 17 against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

The winner of the group will be promoted to League A of the Nations League, while the team finishing second will play a promotion play-off.

Romania managed to gain promotion to League B in the last edition of the Nations League, after winning the group with six wins in the same number of matches. This performance allowed the national team to reach the play-offs for the 2026 World Cup, although they finished third in their group in the qualifiers.

World.title: Bucharest included in ranking of cities with highest potential for AI data center development
World.content:
Romania’s capital ranks 21st in the Savills Power and Place Index, the global ranking that assesses cities with the strongest potential for future data center development based on criteria such as energy availability, telecommunications infrastructure, access to resources and project delivery capability.

According to Savills’s report, the next wave of investment in digital infrastructure will increasingly target markets capable of supporting the accelerated expansion of artificial intelligence. The same report showed that global investment in data centers has reached record levels, fueled by the expansion of major hyperscale operators and growing demand driven by artificial intelligence. In this context, the challenge is no longer the availability of capital, but rather identifying locations capable of providing the power, land and infrastructure required for large-scale developments.

Savills highlighted that many established European hubs are already experiencing limitations related to power grid capacity, land availability and permitting processes, creating opportunities for emerging cities and markets with greater resource availability.

According to real estate consultant Crosspoint Real Estate, Romania benefits from several structural advantages relevant to digital infrastructure development. These include a high level of fiber-optic coverage, competitive internet speeds and affordable data service costs, all of which support large-scale data transfer and processing.

At the same time, data consumption continues to grow rapidly both in Romania and across the Central and Eastern European region, driven by the expansion of cloud services, the digitalization of the economy and the integration of artificial intelligence solutions into business operations. This trend is increasing the need for local and regional digital infrastructure and is supporting the development of data centers located closer to end users.

At present, however, one significant disadvantage is the cost of electricity. Nevertheless, with the commissioning of the Iernut and Mintia power plants, as well as the projected development of energy storage facilities in the medium term, Romania could become increasingly attractive for this segment.

“While traditional European hubs are facing increasing constraints related to energy access, land availability and development restrictions, Bucharest is emerging as a well-positioned market for the next wave of investments in digital infrastructure supporting AI development. For data center investors, access to power and connectivity is becoming just as important as location,” said Emilian Podaru, MRICS, Head of Industrial & Logistics at Crosspoint Real Estate, the International Associate of Savills in Romania.

The report estimated that data center expansion will also have a significant impact on the industrial and logistics sector. Across Europe, the growth of this ecosystem could generate additional demand for approximately 790,000 sq m of logistics space over the next three years, required for storage, equipment, operations, and related services.

World.title: “Seaside for Everyone” program aims to attract tourists to Romanian seaside in September
World.content:
The 49th edition of “Seaside for Everyone,” a well-known program that aims to attract tourists to the Romanian seaside through massive price cuts in accommodation, was announced on Tuesday, August 25, by the Federation of Associations of Romanian Tourism Employers (FPTR).

Initiated and coordinated by FPTR and supported through the participation of economic operators on the seaside, “Seaside for Everyone” advances holidays on the seaside at reduced rates for tourists.

The program takes place from September 1-30, 2026.

To date, 67 accommodation units from 10 resorts and tourist areas are enrolled. According to FPTR, a novelty of this year’s edition is the change in the list of participants. 24 of the units currently enrolled did not participate in the spring edition. Among them are units entering the program for the first time, as well as returning operators.

Moreover, compared with the spring edition, when the lowest rate communicated was RON 42/person/night, the current edition starts at RON 39/person/night for accommodation without meals, in Eforie Nord.

The minimum rates communicated by other participating units are RON 39 (EUR 7.43) in Eforie Nord, RON 65 (EUR 12.38) in Eforie Sud, RON 60 (EUR 11.43) in Costinești, RON 58 (EUR 11.05) in Neptun-Olimp, RON 74 (EUR 14.10) in Jupiter, RON 77 (EUR 14.67) in Saturn, RON 108 (EUR 20.57) in Mangalia, RON 80 (EUR 15.24) in Vama Veche, RON 69 (EUR 13.14) in Mamaia, and RON 65 (EUR 12.38) in Mamaia Nord.

The rates, the included services, and participation periods are established by each accommodation unit. Some offers are for accommodation, while others include breakfast or All Inclusive services. The packages can also be paid for with holiday vouchers, under the conditions accepted by each accommodation unit or travel agency.

Although the official period of the program is September 1–30, 2026, some units have submitted offers that continue into October. As such, tourists have more holiday options in the off-season, while operators can maintain their activity for a longer period.

The list of participating units, rates, validity periods and contact details is published on the official website of the Federation of Associations of Romanian Tourism Employers. The list is updated as FPTR receives new registrations.

World.title: Romanian MP Claudiu Năsui accepts nomination as Moldova’s economy minister
World.content:
Romanian lawmaker Claudiu Năsui accepted prime minister Vasile Tofan’s invitation to join the Moldovan government as minister of economic development and digitalization. The Save Romania Union (USR) deputy said the move would require him to resign from Romania’s Parliament.

“I have accepted the position of economy minister in the government of the Republic of Moldova,” Năsui announced on Facebook. He said he strongly agreed with Tofan’s vision of turning Moldova into “the most welcoming country for entrepreneurs.”

Claudiu Năsui said he would use his experience to support economic reforms, including the liberalization and privatization process started after the fall of communism. He also linked Moldova’s economic development to its efforts to join the European Union and strengthen ties with Romania.

“I chose to accept Mr. Tofan’s invitation to join the government of the Republic of Moldova, even though this step means giving up my mandate as a member of the Romanian Parliament and dedicating my experience to a new reform effort,” Năsui said.

“A more prosperous Moldovan economy also means a more prosperous Romanian economy as part of our shared European path,” he added.

Vasile Tofan announced that Claudiu Năsui would be proposed for the position of minister of economic development and digitalization, citing his economic education, private-sector experience, and previous involvement in government reforms.

Năsui studied economics at Paris Dauphine University and finance at Bocconi University. He has worked in the financial sector, including at PwC and Romanian bank BCR, and holds the Chartered Financial Analyst certification.

He was first elected to the Romanian Parliament in 2016 and served as Romania’s economy minister between 2020 and 2021. He also founded the Open Budget platform, which tracks public spending.

According to prime minister Tofan, Claudiu Năsui’s priorities in Moldova will include reducing bureaucracy, addressing problems at state-owned companies, cutting public expenditure, and removing obstacles faced by small and medium-sized enterprises.

“We need this type of energy at the Economy Ministry,” Vasile Tofan said. “We want the Economy Ministry to become one of the main drivers of state reform and economic growth.”

The Moldovan prime minister also announced that Eugeniu Osmochescu would be proposed as minister of agriculture and food industry. His responsibilities will include preparing Moldovan agriculture for EU accession and improving the sector’s competitiveness and resilience to climate change.

(Photo source: Facebook/Claudiu Nasui)

World.title: Romanian Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner Fjord draws over 150,000 viewers after French release
World.content:
Fjord, the latest film from Romanian director Cristian Mungiu, attracted more than 150,000 viewers shortly after opening in France on August 19. France is the first of more than 100 territories where the Palme d’Or-winning film is due to receive a theatrical release.

The film ranked first in box-office receipts during both its previews and its official opening day, when it was seen by 30,058 people, including 11,727 in Paris, according to a press release. By the end of its first weekend, it had drawn 140,346 viewers in cinemas, with the Paris audience accounting for 51,847 admissions.

Including preview screenings, Fjord reached a total audience of 151,121 across 270 cinemas. Its distribution is expanding to 290 screens this week.

“Based on the ratio between its first-day box-office revenue and final audience figures, Fjord could attract more than 800,000 viewers in France,” reads the announcement.

The film is distributed in France by Le Pacte, which has handled all of Cristian Mungiu’s films since 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days. The latter, which won the filmmaker his first Palme d’Or in 2007, attracted around 380,000 viewers in France.

The release figures place Fjord ahead of the opening-day performance of some other recent Palme d’Or winners. Jafar Panahi’s It Was Just an Accident, the 2025 winner, debuted with 20,000 viewers and eventually reached 700,000 admissions, while Sean Baker’s Anora opened at a level close to Fjord and finished with 654,000 viewers.

Cristian Mungiu’s film won the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival in May, along with the FIPRESCI Prize, the Citizenship Prize, the François Chalais Prize, and the Ecumenical Jury Prize.

Fjord was also shown to 43,440 viewers in Romania during a one-off screening on June 13. Distribution also began in French-speaking Switzerland in August, with releases scheduled for September in Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Greece, Italy, and Belgium.

Fjord tells the story of Lisbet and Mihai Gheorghiu, a married couple who move to a small village on a Norwegian fjord. They soon befriend their neighbors, the Halberg family, while the children of the two households grow close despite differences in upbringing and values. The cast includes Sebastian Stan, Renate Reinsve, Adrian Titieni, Alin Panc, Giulia Nahmany, and Ana Bodea.

World.title: Center-right European groups EPP, Renew ask EC to withhold PNRR funds to Romania over integrity law
World.content:
The leaders of the center-right European People’s Party (EPP) and Renew Europe, two of the most important groups in the European Parliament, publicly asked the European Commission on Monday, August 24, to withhold EUR 770 million in PNRR funds meant for Romania due to the “Fritz amendment.” Their plea concerns the retroactive application of a new integrity law that would invalidate the mandate of Timisoara mayor Dominic Fritz.

EPP president Manfred Weber and Renew group leader Valérie Hayer both signed a letter shared by POLITICO asking Commission president Ursula von der Leyen to make it clear that the money will not be granted unless Bucharest abandons plans to amend a law that could lead to Save Romania Union (USR) party leader Dominic Fritz being banned from holding the office of mayor.

Weber and Hayer also argued that retroactive application violates EU legislation and Romania’s Constitution and accused the Romanian Social Democrats of deliberately targeting Fritz. “Under the guise of fulfilling a reform milestone for the Recovery and Resilience Facility, the Romanian Parliament has introduced a measure that directly violates Union law and constitutes a serious setback for the rule of law in Romania,” they said in the letter.

"European taxpayers’ money must never become a blank check for political power games,” Hayer told POLITICO. Weber added that “if legislation is designed to remove a political opponent, and EU funds are used as leverage to enforce it, this is no longer just politics - it is a rule-of-law issue.”

In the letter, they also urged the Commission to send “a signal” before Romanian president Nicușor Dan promulgates the law and before the August 31 deadline for the reforms that would allow access to EU funds.

The Fritz amendment

Earlier this month, in a 5-3 vote, the Romanian Constitutional Court approved the so-called “Fritz Amendment,” introduced by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) into the law governing the National Integrity Agency (ANI). The same law is a PNRR milestone with EUR 770 million attached to it.

The controversial amendment stipulates that elected officials in office lose their mandate within 30 days if they receive a final decision of incompatibility or conflict of interest, even if this decision predates the new law. This means that the law would apply retroactively. In June, Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Timișoara Court of Appeal ruling that found Dominic Fritz in an administrative conflict of interest.

As such, under the amendment, Fritz is expected to lose his position as mayor of Timișoara within 30 days of the legislation entering into force. The USR leader announced that he will challenge the decision at the European Court of Human Rights, and argued that the measure applies to a past action, although the Romanian Constitution states that laws should apply only to the future.

On course for adoption

After it was declared constitutional, the amended law was returned to Parliament and was adopted by the Chamber of Deputies with the votes of PSD, the National Liberal Party (PNL), and the minority Hungarian party UDMR. It still has to pass the Senate on Wednesday, August 26, and then go to president Nicusor Dan, who previously criticized the same "Fritz amendment," for promulgation before becoming law.

The supporters of the amended bill said its adoption secures EU funding, despite the retroactive application.

"For those who vote to violate the rule of law for fear of losing money from the PNRR: I am sure the European Commission will not accept rewarding such an abusive monstrosity with European taxpayers’ money," Fritz said on Facebook, in reaction to the bill's passing of the Chamber of Deputies.

Since the CCR decision, Fritz was also reconfirmed as leader of USR, which is part of the Renew Europe group in the European Parliament.

(Photo source: Valerie Hayer and Manfred Weber on Facebook)

World.title: Romania’s Patria Bank accelerates lending in Q2 2026, loan portfolio nears RON 3 billion
World.content:
Patria Bank (BVB: PBK), a major Romanian bank listed on the Regulated Market of the Bucharest Stock Exchange, ended the first half of 2026 with a total performing loan portfolio of nearly RON 3 billion, up approximately 12% compared to June 30, 2025.

According to the bank, the evolution was supported by the acceleration of commercial activity in the second quarter across both the legal entities and retail segments.

As of June 30, 2026, the portfolio of performing loans granted to legal entities reached RON 2.40 billion, up 9% compared to the end of 2025 and 13% compared to the same period of the previous year.

The volume of new loans granted to corporate clients accelerated significantly in the second quarter, reaching RON 466 million, 44% above the level recorded in Q2 2025 and 67% higher than in the first quarter of 2026. For the first half of the year as a whole, the volume of new loans granted to corporate clients reached RON 746 million, up 2% compared to the same period of the previous year.

“Our ambition is to become an increasingly relevant bank for the clients we serve and to turn every financing granted into a long-term relationship that evolves alongside their needs,” stated Valentin Vancea, General Manager of Patria Bank.

The Agro segment recorded the fastest growth in the first half of the year, with the performing loan portfolio reaching RON 523 million, 29% above the level recorded as of December 31, 2025. New loan sales in this segment reached RON 224 million, up 35% compared to H1 2025, driven by farmers’ seasonal working capital needs and interest in projects supported by European funds. At the same time, the Bank continued its diversification towards the financing of the food industry, where financing for clients advanced 67% compared to the first half of 2025.

The Micro segment portfolio reached RON 434 million, up 3% compared to the end of 2025. New loan sales in the first half of the year reached RON 114 million, below the high base recorded in the same period of the previous year. The bank expects activity in this segment to record a positive evolution in the coming quarters, supported by adjustments to the analysis flow for financing requirements.

Across the SME and Corporate segments, the performing loan portfolio increased by 4% compared to the end of 2025, reaching RON 1.44 billion. This evolution was mainly driven by the Corporate component, which advanced by 14% in the first six months of the year. The two segments generated new financing of RON 408 million, with a strong recovery in the second quarter.

In the retail segment, the total balance of performing retail loans reached RON 584 million at the end of June, up 9% compared to the same period of the previous year. Unsecured loans remained the main growth driver of the retail portfolio, advancing by 16% to RON 275 million. This evolution was supported by sustained demand for consumer loans and credit cards, as well as by the increasing share of sales generated through digital channels, including the Patria de Oriunde platform. The balance of secured loans also returned to growth, reaching RON 309 million, 3% above the level recorded as of June 30, 2025.

New retail loan sales reached RON 138 million in the first half of the year, up 8.5% compared to H1 2025. Of this volume, RON 80 million was granted in the second quarter, 19% above the same period of the previous year. Sales of secured loans increased by 32% in the first half of the year, reaching RON 29 million, while unsecured loans accounted for approximately 79% of the total volume of new retail loans, with sales of RON 109 million.

In terms of commercial financing, corporate commercial financing increased by 17% compared to the end of 2025 and by 31% compared to June 30, 2025, reaching RON 2.20 billion. Commercial financing related to the retail segment reached RON 2.25 billion, 8% above the level recorded one year earlier. Term deposits reached RON 1.91 billion, while the balance of current accounts increased to RON 338 million.

As of the same date, SAI Patria Asset Management had assets under management of RON 1.53 billion, up 78% compared to December 31, 2025 and 177% compared to June 30, 2025. The financial performance of the two entities is not included in Patria Bank’s individual financial results. After the end of the reporting period, on August 5, 2026, Patria Bank completed the sale to BRD Asset Management SAI of its 99.9944% shareholding in SAI Patria Asset Management. As a result, SAI Patria Asset Management is no longer a subsidiary of Patria Bank.

World.title: European Court Orders Turkey to Release Osman Kavala Immediately, Again
World.content:
The European Court of Human Rights, ECHR, on Tuesday ruled for a second time that Turkey should release the jailed philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala. Judges found that his detention and conviction violated multiple provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights.

“The respondent State was required to secure the applicant’s release at the earliest possible date,” the Court said, adding that Turkey must eliminate the consequences of the measures taken against him. It said Kavala’s criminal conviction should be regarded as “null and void” under the Convention’s provisions.

Kavala is a prominent civil society figure and former board member of the Open Society Foundations in Turkey. He has been in custody since October 2017, facing charges in connection with the 2013 Gezi Park protests and the failed coup attempt of July 2016.

An Istanbul court sentenced Kavala to “aggravated life imprisonment” – without the possibility of release – in April 2022. He was convicted of attempting to overthrow the government through his support for the Gezi Park protests. The months of demonstrations constituted the largest popular uprising against the authoritarian leadership of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Two appeal courts upheld Kavala’s conviction in December 2022 and September 2023.

In its latest ruling, the ECHR found violations of several provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights, including freedom of expression and assembly, the right to a fair trial and the right to liberty and security. It also found that Kavala’s aggravated life sentence without the possibility of release violated Article 3, which explicitly prohibits “torture [and] inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.

Judges concluded that a desire to silence Kavala was behind the criminal proceedings, his conviction and his continued detention. The Turkish authorities aimed to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender.

The judgment follows years of pressure over Turkey’s failure to implement previous ECHR rulings concerning Kavala. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers eventually launched infringement proceedings against Turkey in 2022. That process could ultimately lead to sanctions, including the suspension of voting rights or even membership.

The Court also ordered Turkey to pay Kavala 70,000 euros in non-pecuniary damages and 43,342.57 euros in costs and expenses.

World.title: Kosovo Starts Countdown on KLA Leaders War Crimes Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Countdown monitor installed at Pristina city center photographed on August 24, 2026. Photo: BIRN/ Islam Berisha

The clock is ticking in Ferizaj/Urosevac. Kosovo’s third-largest city now has installed a countdown timer on Monday, which will reach zero on the day that former president Hashim Thaci is due to learn his fate. The capital, Pristina, has a similar installation, with other cities due to follow suit.

Along with three other former senior leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), Thaci is accused of committing crimes against humanity – including murder, torture and illegal detention – during the Kosovo conflict in the late 1990s. Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague are calling for a 45-year prison sentence.

But as far as Ferizaj/Urosevac’s mayor Agim Aliu is concerned, Thaci and his co-defendants – Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi – are heroes of Kosovo’s independence struggle. And he believes the newly-installed timer in the city’s main square is counting down the days to what should be a massive celebration.

“Ferizaj and the entire Kosovo [will] experience September 16 as a new date of freedom,” he says, adding that he expects a “historic verdict” reflecting “the sacrifice” the four defendants made for Kosovo’s freedom.

On Monday, Ferizaj/Urosevac became the second municipality to receive a countdown clock, courtesy of the initiative “Freedom Has a Name” (Liria Ka Emer). It plans to install similar timers in other municipalities around Kosovo.

One of the initiative’s leaders is Eliza Hoxha, an MP representing Thaci’s former party, the PDK (Democratic Party of Kosovo), which is currently in opposition. She says she believes in the four defendants’ innocence.

“Kosovo is waiting, we are all waiting. We will count down hours, minutes, seconds until September 16. Kosovo waits for Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi to once again stamp our right to be free and independent.”

The charges facing the four men are serious. Prosecutors accuse them of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania. Those include more than one hundred murders.

The charges cover the period during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999. All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. As prime minister in 2014, Hashim Thaci signed an agreement with the European Union to establish the court.

It is based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters. Veterans are widely viewed as heroes in Kosovo and the potential for witness intimidation was a serious concern.

During the trial, the prosecution argued that the defendants’ senior roles in the KLA meant they were responsible for subordinates who committed crimes. The defence insisted that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges. Since then, he and his three co-defendants have been in detention in The Hague, with the trial starting in April 2023. KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the KSC of bias.

Prosecutors brought further charges against Thaci In 2024. He and four others, including former Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci, are accused of obstruction of justice and witness tampering. Prosecutors say Thaci and his co-accused attempted to direct witness testimony in his war crimes trial.

The second case went to trial in February this year, just days after proceedings in Thaci’s first trial concluded. All the accused have pleaded not guilty.

World.title: Planned Amazon Warehouse in Czechia Faces Local Resistance, Again
World.content:
August deadline

Now being developed by investors Accolade and Garbe, the land of the Borsov Economic Development Zone I was purchased in 1998, with initial zoning plans banking on the construction of a large shopping centre.

This never materialised, and in 2020 developers received zoning approval for the construction of four smaller, separate industrial halls – two of which already have building permits – for a total built area of over 148,000 square metres. Now, the modalities have changed again.

Accolade and Garbe redesigned the entire project into a single, larger building (77,000 square metres in size, about 500 metres long and 15 metres high) specifically for a single tenant – Amazon – on an expected 20-year-lease agreement. About 2,500 people could be employed there, working on a two-shift rotation running almost non-stop from 06:30 to 04:30.

According to Borsov nad Vltavou’s mayor, Romana Rycova, the municipality was only informed about the change at the end of April. And in a video posted on August 13, Mayor Rycova stated that the municipal council must now approve the new variant by the end of August or the investors will redesign the project so they can bypass the municipality’s approval – despite an earlier promise made to residents to “wait as long as you need”.

Representatives for the investors tell BIRN that their earlier communication might have been misconstrued. “When we said that there would be no time pressure, we meant that we would not push municipal council members towards a particular decision or influence how they vote,” says Tomas Mile, project manager at Accolade.

“It did not mean that the project itself had no commercial timetable,” he says, adding that the municipality had been informed since late 2025 about the changes. Rather than a sudden change, Mile describes the new single-building option as “the gradual development of a new option in response to a specific requirement from a prospective tenant”.

Furthermore, he says that while “we understand the concerns raised by residents”, he makes the case that developers have shown goodwill and transparency over the past several months to explain the differences and varying impacts to local residents.

Amazon did not respond to BIRN’s requests for comment.

However, Horakova says she has attended all the public meetings held over the past several months and describes the communication there from developers as “misleading at best”.

Considering the new parameters of the project, she also believes that fresh independent studies should be conducted to upgrade now-outdated environmental impact studies and properly evaluate the impact of such a massive distribution centre on traffic, air-quality, noise pollution and local landscape preservation – just a few of the main concerns expressed by both residents and city officials over the past several months.

“We’ve found no evidence that these studies have been updated for the new design, including in the investor’s own newest technical documentation,” Horakova explains.

Echoing the thoughts of other locals, Horakova accuses the developers of “not being a trustworthy party”. Case in point, Veronika Zacha – who became Garbe’s senior manager for business development for Czechia after moving from Panattoni in 2022 – promised during an August town hall meeting: “We don’t want to pressure the municipality, we also understand that you need to familiarise yourself with all the information, so you have time.”

Yet shortly afterwards, city councillors received an SMS clarifying that developers expect a decision by the end of the month – or else they will move ahead with the four-hall format, according to information from iRozhlas.cz and other local outlets.

World.title: Across the Balkans, Foreign-Backed Luxury Developments Cause Local Anger
World.content:
Since Albania’s ‘Flamingo Revolution’ protests began in May, they have attracted worldwide attention and sparked debate within and outside the Balkans about high-profile investors’ mega-projects.

The protests began in response to the proposed luxury tourism projects on Albania’s Sazan Island and the Zvernec protected coastline. The 1.4 and 4.7 billion euro investments are being led by Affinity Partners, an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Kushner and his wife Ivanka Trump first visited Albania in 2021 and announced plans for the development in 2024.

There has been much to anger locals about the projects, including comments Ivanka Trump made on a podcast where she referred to “discovering” Sazan Island and called the state-owned land a “private island”.

Another more substantive issue is that the Albanian government amended the laws on protected areas on February 22, 2024, allowing five-star hotels to be built inside protected areas. This occurred a month before Kushner’s Albanian projects were announced.

World.title: As Turkey Makes Peace, Kurdish Villagers Who Fled Conflict Contemplate Return
World.content:
“It was the biggest breaking point in my life,” said Aydin Kurdis, remembering the day he and his family left their village 32 years ago.

In the early 1990s, the village of Golord, known officially as Bostancik, was home to around 200 families. Its stone houses sat among hills covered with walnut and fruit trees. Villagers made a living raising livestock, while the orchards provided much of what families needed.

“Before we left the village, I didn't know what pain was. I didn't know what poverty was,” Kurdis said, sitting in front of the house where he was born and eating cucumbers just pulled from the garden down the slope on an August afternoon. “Life was hard on us after we moved to the city.”

Kurdis, 52, lives in Yuksekova, the largest district in Turkey’s southeastern Hakkari province, near the Iranian border. Golord is only a 45-minute drive away, but the final 10 kilometres are unpaved, with potholes dotting the dusty mountain road.

World.title: Experts Warn Proposed Limits on Serbian Officials Campaigning Will Be Ineffective
World.content:
Serbia’s parliament began a debate on amendments to the Law on the Prevention of Corruption on Monday – changes the government says will regulate political campaigning by public officials.

But the anti-corruption watchdog Transparency Serbia claims the measures are unlikely to be effective.

Transparency Serbia said the amendments “create the appearance that restrictions are being introduced, while in practice they will have virtually no effect”.

The watchdog pointed out that the OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) has identified campaigning by public officials as “a key element in blurring the line between the party and the state” in Serbia.

It noted that restrictions would apply only after the publication of electoral lists, and focus solely on the conduct of officials who have been nominated as candidates. As a result, the period before this remains unregulated.

It said this allows officials to use “pseudo-events” like school, hospital and construction site tours to campaign, as long as visits were arranged “before the elections were called”.

With advance notice of election dates, government candidates could schedule events “precisely for the period leading up to the elections, even though these events serve no purpose other than promotion.”

Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic has yet to name the precise date for early parliamentary elections, though he has said they will be held in October.

In the meantime, he has embarked on a prolific schedule of visits around the country. Videos from those events appear on media outlets and social networks, showing local people asking the president about infrastructure works and job opportunities. Vucic has also announced numerous giveaways for Serbian adults, alongside a range of subsidies.

This is precisely what Transparency Serbia has in mind with its definition of “promotional activity” by a public official. It says the draft amendments also fail to address ODIHR delivered recommendations on restricting “extraordinary spending by state institutions ahead of elections”.

The watchdog claims that this “helicopter money” – including various measures planned by the government, such as salary increases, lower medicine prices and one-off payments to various different sectors of society – will amount to almost one billion euros by the time the elections are held.

World.title: Translation Cutbacks Limit International Access to North Macedonia’s Literature
World.content:
For a small country of just under two million people, with a small language and an even smaller literary market, getting books translated and published abroad can be crucial to keeping its literature visible beyond its borders.

But for the past two years, Macedonian authors and publishers have had one fewer tool to help them do that. A government programme that provided grants to foreign publishers willing to translate and publish Macedonian books has been suspended since 2024.

The good news is that the Culture Ministry told BIRN there is a “real possibility” it will relaunch a redesigned translation programme later this year. But the bad news is how many excellent books have been denied a wider readership over the last two years.

The Ministry says it typically allocated between one to four million denars [16,000- 65,000 euros] a year for the programme. In 2024, around 84,000 euros was distributed through 31 contracts with foreign publishers. Foreign publishers interested in Macedonian literature could apply to North Macedonia’s Culture Ministry for funding to cover translation costs, reducing the financial risk of publishing authors who are largely unknown in their markets.

Without that incentive, publishers say, some potentially valuable translations simply do not happen. “Our success at international book fairs, such as Frankfurt, is diminished,” says Bojan Sazdov, editor-in-chief of the publishing house TRI and president of the Macedonian Association of Publishers.

“When there is interest in translating a Macedonian book, we can no longer point publishers to the programme as a way of obtaining funding for the translation.”

World.title: August 25th 1991 – The Battle of Vukovar Begins
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – On August the 25th, 1991, the battle of Vukovar began, marking the start of one of the most devastating chapters of the Croatian War of Independence.

The most harrowing episode of the Homeland War began on this day in the eastern Croatian city of Vukovar when members of the JNA from the barracks in Vukovar joined Serbian paramilitary units. After doing so, they jointly launched an attack on both Borovo and Vukovar. Index writes that the siege lasted 87 days and transformed Vukovar into a symbol of Croatian resistance and heroism during the Homeland War.

the initial conflicts begin

Slobodan Milošević – NATO

After Croatia declared independence on the 25th of June 1991, local conflicts in eastern Slavonia had already begun. For centuries Vukovar had been a city where Croats, Serbs and Hungarians lived in peace, but the situation changed at the end of the 1980s with the rise of nationalism and the policies of Slobodan Milošević, who wanted to consolidate power in Belgrade.

On the 25th of August, the JNA left the barracks with six tanks that blocked the road towards Bogdanovci. The very next day a new attack on Borovo began that lasted the entire day. The firing briefly stopped, and already during the following night another offensive started. By the 30th of August, the clashes continued one after another, after which a short ceasefire occurred during which weapons were delivered to the Croats in Vukovar from Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci and Zagreb. At that time Mile Dedaković arrived in Vukovar and organised the army and defensive positions in the city.

the serbs wanted to go all the way to zagreb

The JNA commander in Vukovar was Života Panić, who wanted to capture Vukovar as quickly as possible in order to prevent further mobilisation of the Croatian army. The original JNA plan was to take Vukovar and Osijek, then occupy all of Slavonia so that the road towards Varaždin and Zagreb would be open. However, problems already appeared when fewer than two thousand Croatian soldiers withstood numerous JNA attacks in Vukovar.

The plan was not helped by the fact that only 13% of those fit for military service responded to the call-up. After news arrived of the large number of casualties in Vukovar, many soldiers deserted, and by the end of 1991 there were six thousand open court proceedings against deserters. The failure of mobilisation meant the cancellation of the grandiose conquest of the whole of continental Croatia, culminating with Zagreb.

the fall of vukovar and horrific crimes against humanity

Vukovar endured a three-month siege in which seven thousand projectiles fell daily. On the 18th of November the city fell, although only 10–15% of the buildings actually remained. The rest were entirely destroyed. The army entered the city and the expulsion of the non-Serb population and horrific war crimes and crimes against humanity began. Neighbours accused other neighbours of being a defender, informed on where families were located, and just a few days later more than 250 civilians were brutally killed at Ovčara in one single night.

The sight of the murder of hundreds of innocent civilians – Perun

The total number of victims is measured in the thousands of people, and there are probably other undiscovered mass graves containing those who disappeared during the war. The Serbian government under Aleksandar Vučić refuses to cooperate so that the remaining mysteries from the war can finally be resolved.

The city was returned to Croatia only in 1998 through peaceful reintegration, and the 18th of November is marked in Croatia as the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Homeland War. Vukovar has still not recovered from the war: today it has just over 25,000 inhabitants, while in the years before the war it was home to 45,000 people. As the largest Croatian port on the Danube, Vukovar was a busy centre of trade and transport.

Today. it is only a shadow of what it once was, and Croatian authorities from the 1990s until today have not invested enough in it. It was the fifth-largest city in the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, then larger even than Zadar, while today it is not ranked among the ten largest Croatian cities.

World.title: Croatia is Full of Tourists, But “Coolcations” Are Increasingly Popular
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia remains full of tourists, but with horrifically hot temperatures now the norm, “coolcations” pose a serious threat to hotter countries as they become increasingly popular.

The director of the Croatian National Tourist Board, Kristjan Staničić, said that there are still more than a million tourists per day in Croatia and that August is so far at the level of last year’s results. Index reports that when speaking on HRT’s Dnevnik, Staničić said that Croatia is still at the peak of the tourist season, but he did not want to forecast what August would be like until the end. “For now I can say that August is at the level of last year’s figures,” he said.

“coolcations” are becoming more and more popular as people tire of overwhelming heat

Staničić also commented on a new tourist trend, the so-called “coolcation”, or the growing interest in cooler destinations in northern Europe. As he explained, because of ever higher summer temperatures and repeated heatwave cycles, many people are looking for places where July and August are more pleasant than on the Mediterranean and in southern Europe. He believes this trend will continue in the coming years and that the tourism sector must be prepared for it. He recalled that climate change has been affecting travellers’ decisions for a longer time, but considers that Croatia, thanks to its diverse offer, can respond to such changes as well.

As an example he mentioned Gorski kotar and Lika, where lower temperatures, quality accommodation, good gastronomy and contents linked to nature and active holidays can be found even during the summer.

inspectors clamp down on illegal rentals and s

Staničić also commented on the intensified work of the tourist inspection this season. Because of illegal operation, eight campsites, 23 holiday homes, 56 apartments, one smaller hotel and one hostel have been closed. He thanked the staff of the State Inspectorate and everyone involved in combating the black market. “Unfortunately, this is a phenomenon that is present and to which a response is needed,” he said. He added that cooperation of all institutions, tourist boards and competent services in the field is important, especially when there is knowledge of unregistered guests or facilities that provide services without being registered for it.

croatian tourism requires proper order

Staničić also spoke about the amendments to the Hospitality Activity Act, against which the Association “Save Small Family Renters” has submitted an objection to the European Commission. They object, among other things, to re-categorisation every decade, the need for co-owners’ consent in multi-apartment buildings, and the conditions for obtaining host status. Staničić expects the law primarily to help in combating the black market.

As one of the most important novelties he singled out the introduction of a registration number that every accommodation service provider will have to have if they want to advertise on global platforms. According to him, such a system should enable more effective control of both accommodation facilities and the online platforms on which they are advertised.

“Everyone has the right to turn to the European Commission,” Staničić said, adding that Croatia has taken over the European acquis which includes the introduction of a registration number. He assessed that this measure should be one of the key tools for combating the black market and “introducing order into Croatian tourism”.

World.title: Croatian Railway Ambitions Tie in With European Defence Efforts
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatian railway ambitions are closely linked with European defence efforts, as the country’s “decade of the railway” is still not really being felt on the ground by most.

Any reason for the renewal and development of the railway system in Croatia is very useful, including the security and defence one. But its civilian role remains primary. Index/Deutsche Welle/Igor Lasic reports that following two serious railway traffic incidents at the beginning of this month in Croatia, this mode of passenger and freight transport is once again a topic for the Croatian public.

Moreover, the general public has been reminded of the fact that Croatia is apparently currently in the middle of its “decade of the railway”. This is a state project for the development of this long-neglected mode of transport, with an investment of six billion euros for new tracks and vehicles. Yet despite years of reconstruction, the results are still not really visible on the ground, even though some concrete works have long been planned. The announced “railway renaissance” will therefore clearly still have to wait, and the recent traffic accidents have uncomfortably highlighted this uncertainty.

On top of everything, a new element has been included in the reasoning for the renewal of the Croatian railway sector, and that’s the wider European defence system. Europe is rapidly arming itself, and Croatia has also bought, among other things, more than 40 German Leopard 2 tanks. These, however, because of their exceptional weight, require equally exceptional railway transport capacities. All of this ultimately enters into the final calculation of the development project of the public company Croatian Railways. On the other hand, its relative urgency and the need for centralisation of the system somewhat remove the possibility of imminent privatisation of the sector, which until recently was quite realistic.

so long, privatisation

“Only through the security sphere and social cohesion around the issue of defence have we come to the conclusion that the railway must be managed by the state if we want an efficient system,” Ante Klečina, a railway expert and lecturer at the Department of Sustainable Mobility and Logistics of the University Sjever (North) in Koprivnica and Varaždin, told DW. He referred to the experience of some more developed European countries, such as Great Britain, whose experiments with railway privatisation ended rather ignominiously. Services became of poor quality and too expensive, the system failed in various aspects, and over time it was abandoned.

“First and foremost should be their functionality for civilian needs and, in fact, the organisation of civilisation,” Klečina continues, “which is relevant at every moment if we do not put that priority out of our minds. Whoever swears by the advantages of market mechanisms forgets that they are not developmentally suitable for large public systems, those that enable basic requirements.” In his opinion, the same applies to other elementary systems, e.g. healthcare, education and the judiciary, etc. The private sector, says Klečina, can be a supplement in certain segments, but the backbone must remain public.

“The reason is the necessity of central planning of such systems, as well as their primarily non-profit task, but also the need for enormous investments for which private individuals usually have neither the capacity nor the interest. Having seen this in practice, Europe has recently abandoned the idea of privatising railways, and the defence topic came afterwards as an additional reason,” considers Ante Klečina, formerly president of the Railway Alliance in the Republic of Croatia. He further notes that this mode of transport has no equal with regard to a series of key factors: above all overall cost-effectiveness, economic multiplier effects and environmental suitability.

central planning will always be needed

Socioeconomist Toni Prug, for his part, believes that behind the question of Croatian railways lies the general problem of political and scientific rejection of planning and public production as a relic of the past. That past concerns the period of socialism and Yugoslavia, and everything connected with it remained at the very least stigmatised after the war in Croatia. “In reality, however, all successful states are huge public production systems,” says Prug, “in which planning decides on the largest budgets within economies, on interventions whose importance for the population surpasses the importance of decisions that market actors make.”

This assistant professor at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Rijeka highlights the rule in business that when a market actor makes a mistake, i.e. when things go badly, competition replaces him. “And railways, like all other production systems of a public character that are physically fixed and have monopoly status, need to be carefully planned. Mistakes are much harder to correct. They are also managed differently, different parameters are optimised, a focus on profit does not help. It often cannot even be the goal; the goals are determined by the plan.” At the same time the question arises of whether the Republic of Croatia has the professional staff for designing and implementing this.

“private goals have prevailed over practicality”

“Our profession and managerial staff are educated through faculty and professional curricula that say almost nothing about why and how to produce systems and services of a public character, and why they are superior for certain needs,” Prug is convinced, adding that this knowledge still exists in some Croatian public systems, while in others it has collapsed and been left to spontaneity. In his assessment, the City of Zagreb represents a recent example in Croatia that planning can return and capacities be rebuilt. And on higher-quality, data- and analysis-based foundations, which does not concern the railway but can be a general model.

Toni Prug, who in his scientific work has dealt quite a bit with the topic of public sector management, finally conveyed to us the impression that Croatian Railways have so far been a kind of victim of the oil and automobile lobby. “Their private and profit goals have prevailed over the practicality, efficiency, safety and ecological superiority of modern railway systems,” he told DW. Such a hierarchy could change soon thanks to military priorities. But the future of the railway and of social development in general will certainly not be bright if its primarily civilian advantages remain somewhere beside the tracks.

World.title: Croatia Among European Record Holders for Firefighter Numbers
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is among the European record holders when it comes to firefighter numbers as the overall number within Europe has fallen.

Poslovni reports that the total number of firefighters across the EU fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a year that was the worst in EU history in terms of burned area.

Croatia is among the European record holders for firefighter numbers, holding one of the highest shares of professional firefighters in employment in the entire EU. Back in 2025, they accounted for 0.43 percent of total employment, making Croatia second among the 22 EU Member States for which data has been made available. This places Croatia right behind Greece (0.47 percent), according to Euronews. The EU average was 0.18 percent. Portugal follows with 0.33 percent, while the lowest shares are recorded by the Netherlands (0.05), Austria (0.07) and Sweden (0.10 percent).

Across the entire EU there were around 372,400 professional firefighters. Germany had the most, 57,700, followed by France with 47,700 and Italy with 43,500. Next come Poland with 40,000 and Spain with 38,500; the four largest EU economies together account for 187,400 firefighters, or 50.3 percent of the total number. The overall figure in the Union fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a single year that was the worst in EU history for burned areas. The European Trade Union Confederation and EPSU call this drop “reckless cuts” and note that Poland lost 9,000 and France lodt 4,100 firefighters.

Croatia doesn’t rank among the leaders in total numbers, but its share of total employment is among the highest. Eurostat data refers to professional firefighters, including forest firefighters, but not volunteer firefighters. The data also doesn’t show precisely how many professional firefighters are specialised specifically in fighting open-air fires.

The data comes at a time when Europe is facing an ever-growing fire risk. According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) by the 13th of August, the figure had risen to 568,415 hectares from 1,647 fires. For comparison, 2025 was the most destructive season ever recorded in the EU, with 1,079,538 hectares burned in 25 of the 27 EU Member States.

For 2026 the EU has secured a fleet of 22 firefighting aircraft and five helicopters, and in the event of major fires member states can request additional firefighters and equipment through the European Civil Protection Mechanism. In addition, a record 777 firefighters from 14 European countries have been pre-positioned in Cyprus, Greece, Italy, France, Spain and Portugal. Croatia contributes two medium amphibious aircraft to the European fleet, and in 2026 the Commission is also opening a new regional firefighting base in Cyprus with capacity for six aircraft.

World.title: Zadar Was the Most Expensive Croatian City in July
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Zadar was the most expensive Croatian city of all in July, with strong economic growth very much being a double edged sword for the area.

Buying basic groceries has long been a negotiation with one’s own wallet for people in Croatia, but in July, the toughest conditions spilled over onto the area of Zadar County. The basic consumer basket for a four-member family here reached a record 498 euros, reports HRT. Morski writes that a basic daily trip to the shop or the market has become a source of stress for many, and citizens openly complain about the constant quiet price rises:

a previously bustling market sits almost empty

“Vegetables have become very expensive, they get used up quickly, you need a lot of them. Fruit is also very expensive and it seems to me that meat has gone up, fish has also gone up a lot,” says Zadar resident Katja. For pensioners, the situation is even more alarming. Every single purchase requires calculation and a search for discounts: “I really don’t go to the shops much. You buy where you can according to your wallet and that’s it, and yes it’s expensive, it’s definitely expensive, this isn’t for us pensioners, it’s abnormal,” is the honest assessment of Zorica, who lives on the Zagreb–Zadar route.

That consumer habits are changing and that people are buying significantly less than in previous years was confirmed to us by the sellers themselves. Zadar’s market, which in July should be bustling with local and foreign visitors, at times looks unusually empty.

Seller Rada briefly summarises the problem: “Everything is expensive, the shops too.” Her colleague Ilonka points out that even regular customers have thinned out their visits: “There are no customers. I normally have my own customers, but look, two people are walking through the market.”

the price of rapid expansion

How did it come about that Zadar took the top spot for the most expensive groceries? Experts explain that the answer lies in a specific economic effect of the rapid expansion of the regional economy.

Assoc. Prof. Dr. Jurica Bosna, Head of the Department of Economics at the University of Zadar, clarifies the background to this trend: “Nobody wants to have the most expensive basket of goods, but it still shows that the county is developing strongly, and this is an effect known in economics, when we grow faster than we perhaps should according to some optimal economic rates, then it’s unfortunately inevitable that inflation will develop and that the result will be like this,” he stated.

While macroeconomic indicators record the growth and development of the whole of Zadar County, for the general public, that statistic brings no comfort whatsoever. The vicious circle in which the economy advances strongly while prices rise in an unbridled way leaves the deepest mark on household budgets. Since wages and pensions do not come close to keeping pace, the consumer baskets of Zadar residents remain ever emptier.

World.title: Meet the Croatian Road Often Compared to the Legendary Route 66
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – There’s an incredibly scenic Croatian road frequently compared to the legendary Route 66 across the pond in the USA – and a drive along it is nothing less than breathtaking.

When someone mentions Route 66, most people immediately think of the endless American highway, old motels, neon signs and kilometres of asphalt running through some of the most famous landscapes of the United States. Few realise that Croatia has its own very interesting road with the same number in Croatia as well. It goes without saying that Croatia’s D66 doesn’t have thousands of kilometres or hold the status of an American icon, but because of the designation it carries and the landscapes it passes through, it resembles the US legend in many ways.

Putni kofer writes that it has been referred to many times as the Istrian version of Route 66 and presented it as a road that evokes old, nostalgic Istria. Today, the impressive D66 connects Pula, Labin and Vozilići with Opatija, and according to the official decision on the classification of public roads it is about 90 kilometres long. Still, if the goal is to find its most spectacular part, one should head towards the eastern coast of Istria, that is, towards Plomin.

the most impressive section begins at plomin

Plomin is an excellent place to start this short road trip. The old fortified little town sits on a hill above Plomin Bay, and right by the D66 there is also a rest area with a viewpoint. A few kilometres further on there is another spot from which the view opens towards the Kvarner Bay, Cres and Lošinj.

After that begins the stretch that makes it worth driving this road slowly. The asphalt winds under the slopes of Učka, the sea is almost constantly somewhere in sight, and on the other side of the Kvarner Cres appears. In certain places the road runs high enough above the coast that the view feels almost like from a large natural balcony. The greatest advantage of state road D66 is precisely that, over a relatively short distance, viewpoints, medieval places, steep coastline and well-known Kvarner resorts alternate.

the stunning Brseč, a town from 1102 towering above at 157 metres above the sea

SONY DSC

One of the places worth turning off the road for is Brseč. D66 reaches it after driving along the slopes of Učka, and the old part of the settlement is situated on a cliff 157 metres high above the expanse of Kvarner. The first written records of Brseč date back to 1102, although the area was inhabited much earlier. It is particularly interesting that the history of Brseč is also directly linked to the road that passes this way. The Tourist Board of Mošćenička Draga notes that the economic development of the place in the 19th century was spurred by the new road from Pula towards Plomin, then Brseč and Mošćenice and further towards Rijeka.

Today the medieval character of Brseč can still be felt in the narrow streets and passages of the old town core. From the cliff by the little church of St Magdalene one of the most beautiful views in the area opens up, while from the western entrance to the place Cres can be seen. Beneath the high rocks a completely different world is hidden. Between Brseč and Mošćenička Draga lie the beaches of Uboka and Jelenšćica, which can be reached on foot via paths that descend from the main road. The coastline in this area is extremely indented, with steep cliffs, tiny coves and stone fishermen’s cottages by the sea.

from ancient towns to well-known resorts

After Brseč the scenery changes again. D66 continues towards Mošćenička Draga, one of the best-known places at the foot of Učka. The road approaches the sea, and the high rocks gradually give way to beaches and a more built-up coastline. Mošćenička Draga developed from a fishing harbour, and today it is especially known for the long pebble beach of Sipar. Its pebbles were formed by the action of the stream that descends from the slopes of Učka and the sea that has shaped them over the years.

Just a few kilometres further on lies Medveja, another place along the D66 with a long pebble beach. After it comes Lovran, where the whole drive takes on a more elegant appearance. Instead of the almost wild coast around Brseč, old villas, gardens and houses appear along the road that recall the time when this part of the Kvarner became one of the favourite resorts of Central Europe.

just over 90 kilometres from pula to opatija

The entire D66 from Pula to Opatija is a little over 90 kilometres long, but for a panoramic outing the stretch from Plomin to Opatija is especially interesting. According to the kilometres listed on the EuroVelo 8 route, from the Plomin area to Opatija it is roughly thirty kilometres of driving.

That may not sound like much, but that is precisely the charm of this road. In a short drive one passes Plomin Bay, open views towards Cres and Lošinj, medieval Brseč, the steep slopes of Učka, Mošćenička Draga, Medveja, Lovran and finally Opatija. Although it forms part of the Croatian cycling route EuroVelo 8, this road should not be imagined as a lonely carriageway without cars. On the official route website traffic on certain sections is marked as moderate, and from Medveja towards Rijeka as heavy, so if you decide to cover it on four wheels, extra caution is recommended for cyclists.

World.title: Drniš Bypass Construction to Benefit Šibenik Port
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – The future Drniš bypass will greatly benefit the local economy, as well as Šibenik Port directly.

The construction of the second and third phases of the complex Drniš bypass project has begun, with the client being Hrvatske ceste (Croatian roads), and the contractor being the consortium of Texo Molior from Cavtat and CGP Slovenia.

Transport Minister Butković pointed out that after securing the financial structure and signing the contract, work on the project is now starting. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that he also noted that it is a technically complex intervention with a route that includes two overpasses, two viaducts and a bridge over the Čikola River. Speaking about the continuation of activities on the future Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, Minister Butković highlighted that the preparation of project documentation for the section from Drniš towards the Oklaj interchange is in an advanced stage.

a 34 million euro investment

After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, so the project is being gradually prepared for phased implementation. He also referred to the reconstruction of state roads DC56 and DC33, which connect the Drniš area with Split and Knin respectively, and whose total reconstruction value is around 34 million euros. After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, gradually preparing the project for implementation.

“A tender has already been issued for one, the other is in preparation, so there will be a great deal of investment in road infrastructure here in the area of the town of Drniš and Šibenik-Knin County,” added Minister Butković. Šibenik-Knin County Prefect Paško Rakić stressed that the Drniš bypass is of great importance for the entire county, especially for the traffic connection of its hinterland, and that residents of the wider Drniš and Knin areas will use it.

“The Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, as well as this bypass, is the backbone of Šibenik-Knin County in terms of traffic, and it is as important to us as the Pelješac Bridge,” emphasised Prefect Rakić. “This is historic for us,” emphasised Drniš Mayor Tomislav Dželalija, noting that generations of Drniš residents have waited decades for this project.

a massive development boost for the area

Expressing satisfaction that the works were ceremonially started today, he pointed out that the removal of transit traffic, along with increased traffic safety, will create additional preconditions for the expansion of the economic zone and the further development of the town. He added that the Government of the Republic of Croatia, through strong investments including road and railway infrastructure, is giving impetus to the town’s development, and thanked them for the projects being implemented in the Drniš area.

President of the Management Board of Hrvatske ceste Ivica Budimir emphasised that the project has a broader economic significance for Drniš, especially because of the direct connection of the industrial zone with the Šibenik port.

“After this road is constructed, the industrial zone in the entire Drniš area will develop significantly faster, better and to a higher quality, and become much more competitive,” emphasised Budimir. Speaking about the technical demands of the project, he added that almost ten percent of the route consists of viaducts, while the most significant structure is the large bridge over the Čikola River canyon, with a span of 220 metres, along with a series of other structures along the route.

World.title: Baćina Lakes – Meet Croatia’s Freshwater Phenomenon
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Baćina Lakes are Croatia’s freshwater phenomenon, with water warmer than that in the sea and the ability to swim year-round.

If you’ve ever driven from Makarska down toward Dubrovnik, you’ll have passed by them. You probably glanced left for a second, spotted a blue patch amid the greenery, and continued on toward the sea. Yet there, just a few kilometres from Ploče, lies something no other Croatian town has: seven lakes within the boundaries of a single town. They are called the Baćina Lakes and bear names that sound like a list from an old book: Oćuša, Crniševo, Podgora, Sladinac, Šipak, Plitko Lake, and Vrbnik.

Putni kofer writes that six of them are interconnected by narrow passages, so you can paddle or boat from one into another, while Vrbnik, which is also the smallest, is completely separate from the rest. Together they cover about 138 hectares.

they’re warmer than the sea

The Baćina Lakes form a cryptodepression, meaning their surface is only slightly above sea level, while their bottoms lie deep below it. Although they are just a step from the sea and surrounded by permeable limestone, the lakes are freshwater. Some springs are nevertheless directly connected to the sea, so salt water appears in the deeper layers. In the Klokun area near Plitko Lake there is a spring that supplies drinking water to the town of Ploče and the surrounding area.

During the scorching summer, the water in the lakes is noticeably warmer than the sea, with tourist sources citing a difference of roughly three degrees. Because of this, the swimming season here starts earlier and ends later than on the coast. The best-known bathing spots are those near the Mindel spring, and the hidden coves and small beaches are reached by kayak, paddleboard, or traditional Neretva boat.

links with queen teuta

Legend has it that the Illyrian Queen Teuta adored this area, and the lakes are still called Teuta’s pearls. Historians, however, have their own evidence and explanations. Near Sladinac Lake the remains of the Roman settlement of Praetoria have been found, along with the remains of an early Christian basilica from the 6th century and a necropolis of stećci tombstones.

Around the lakes a walking and cycling path about 15 kilometres long has been arranged, with benches, springs, and information boards. In 2020 the Public Institution for Protected Natural Areas of Dubrovnik-Neretva County installed 19 educational boards about dragonflies, amphibians, reptiles, and birds. Near the Oćuša spring there is a bird-watching hide, and the lakes also contain three small islets, one of which is named the Island of Love. The entire area forms part of the Natura 2000 ecological network, within two zones of the Neretva Delta, as a habitat for strictly protected and endemic species.

a worthwhile stop off on a long drive south…

A visit to the Baćina Lakes is truly an experience you will remember for a lifetime. Walking the paths that wind right beside the lakes will reveal scenes covered in water lilies, the reflection of clouds mirrored on the still water, and the song of rare birds that creates an almost meditative atmosphere.

Here you can also swim in crystal-clear water that provides refreshment during the great heat, and a special experience comes when the sun sets and the whole landscape is immersed in golden and pink tones. Then the lakes take on an almost fairy-tale appearance. It is a perfect moment for a photograph, but also for simply enjoying the silence of nature.

In the heart of the summer season, a parking space at the viewpoint along the main road is almost impossible to find. Down by the lakes themselves, however, there are usually no crowds. Most travellers photograph the view and drive on, while those who go down to the water, sit in a boat, or cycle a loop are completely enchanted and, like us, probably think: “How is this place not far better known?”

World.title: Vanemuine and the Latvian National Opera swap stages for guest performances this week
World.content:
A guest‑performance exchange between the national theatre Vanemuine and the Latvian National Opera and Ballet begins on Tuesday in Tartu and Riga.

On Tuesday and Wednesday, audiences at Vanemuine's Grand Building can see two guest productions from Latvia. On Tuesday, 25 August, the Latvian National Opera presents Gaetano Donizetti's "L'elisir d'amore", staged by Austrian director Sven‑Eric Bechtolf. The musical director of the production is Mārtiņš Ozoliņš, chief conductor of the Latvian National Opera.

On Wednesday, 26 August, a full house will see Carl Orff's ballet "Carmina Burana", choreographed by Edward Clug, whose short ballet "The Rite of Spring" premiered this spring at Vanemuine. The production brings together the Latvian National Ballet, the Latvian National Opera orchestra and choir, and opera soloists.

In Riga, Vanemuine will perform three productions for Latvian audiences. The tour begins on 27 August at the Dailes Theatre with the drama "The End". On 28 August, the Latvian National Opera hosts Petr Zuska's dance‑music‑theatre piece "Prayer. A Tribute to Arvo Pärt", inspired by the composer's music. On 29 August, audiences will see George Frideric Handel's baroque opera "Julius Caesar", directed by Elmo Nüganen.

Vanemuine director Aivar Mäe said the cooperation is a true cultural bridge between Estonia and Latvia. "One should not wait for the world to come visiting — one must also set out on the road. Vanemuine must stay in motion. And on this bridge, traffic goes both ways," he said.
