World.title: Tigress Umit Shows Signs of Successful Adaptation in Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash Reserve
World.content:
ASTANA – Tigress Umit, released into Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve on July 31 as part of the country’s tiger reintroduction program, is showing positive signs of adapting to the wild, Anuarbek Bermagambetov, head of the Department of Hunting Management and Wildlife, said on the Jibek Joly TV channel on Aug. 24.

More than 70 years after tigers disappeared from Kazakhstan, the predator has returned as part of a long-term reintroduction effort.

Umit’s first recorded prey was a wolf, followed several days later by a wild boar. According to Bermagambetov, her hunting behavior in the first 10 days suggests she is adapting well to her new environment.

Her movements are monitored around the clock with a GPS tracker that transmits her location and direction of travel every 12 hours. Specialists still need to conduct field visits to identify the prey species she catches, as GPS data alone cannot determine this.

Strict monitoring and safety measures

The tigress is currently staying within the reserve’s designated green zone, which covers her main habitat and hunting grounds and poses no immediate threat to nearby settlements.

The reserve covers more than 450,000 hectares, and unauthorized access is prohibited.

The area around Umit has been divided into green, yellow and red zones. If she moves towards the yellow zone, a specially formed conflict-management team will begin monitoring the situation. The team is equipped with three vehicles, a snowmobile, an ATV, night-vision devices, a satellite phone and Starlink.

If Umit enters the red zone, authorities will issue an alert and notify residents of nearby settlements through mobile warnings.

Specialists will initially attempt to drive the tiger back into the green zone using sound and, if necessary, pyrotechnic devices. Temporary sedation is also available as a last resort.

Reintroduction program underway since 2010

Kazakhstan’s tiger reintroduction program has been underway since 2010. The project has included establishing the Ile-Balkhash reserve, restoring its wildlife population and developing the infrastructure needed to support the species’ return.

Two tigers, Bogdan and Puma, were previously brought from the Netherlands in 2024, while Russia transferred four more tigers to Kazakhstan this year. Umit is one of the four animals Russia sent under a bilateral agreement.

Before her release, specialists assessed the reserve’s food base. The area is home to potential tiger prey, including kulan, wild boar, roe deer and Bukhara deer.

Authorities say Umit’s ability to hunt and feed independently is an encouraging early sign that the tigress is adapting to life in the wild.

Officials have also urged the public not to rely on unverified social media footage. Videos of Bogdan and Puma have previously been falsely circulated as footage of Umit, highlighting the growing problem of AI-generated and misleading wildlife content online.

World.title: Adilet Wins Kurultai Elections with 71.17% of Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – The Adilet party secured a landslide victory in Kazakhstan’s Kurultai elections, winning 71.17% of the vote and 110 seats, according to the final results announced by the Central Election Commission (CEC) on Aug. 25.

The electoral rolls included 12,623,289 voters, and 9,351,539 cast ballots. Voter turnout stood at 74.08%.

Adilet received 6,528,948 votes (71.17%) and secured 110 seats in the Kurultai. The Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party won 574,621 votes (6.26%) and 10 seats, while Respublica received 509,631 votes (5.56%) and secured nine seats.

The Aq Zhol Democratic Party garnered 478,083 votes (5.21%) and eight seats. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party received 469,058 votes (5.11%) and also secured eight seats.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 285,395 votes (3.11%), while the Baytaq Green Party garnered 97,751 votes (1.07%). Both parties failed to clear the statutory 5% electoral threshold.

A total of 2.51% of voters selected the “against all” option.

Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, political parties must secure at least 5% of the vote to qualify for seats in the Kurultai. Five parties crossed the threshold based on the final results.

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary election held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system. The 145-member Kurultai replaced the country’s former bicameral Parliament under the Constitution that took effect July 1.

World.title: Nigeria, Sierra Leone See Sharp Rise in Business Registrations in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – The number of companies with founders from Nigeria and Sierra Leone registered in Kazakhstan increased sharply in July.

The number of Nigerian-founded companies rose by 68, while companies with founders from Sierra Leone rose by 45, the Data Hub analytical Telegram channel reported on Aug. 14.

The figures come as Kazakhstan expands economic engagement with African countries. Trade, logistics, agriculture, mining, investment and digital technologies are among the areas of cooperation. Kazakhstan is also developing a Strategy for Cooperation with African States and the African Union for 2025-2030.

Nigeria remains African leader

The number of companies with Nigerian founders increased from 359 on July 1 to 427 on Aug. 1, a 19% rise.

Nigeria has the largest number of registered companies in Kazakhstan among African countries and ranks 21st among all countries represented in the registry.

All Nigerian-founded companies are classified as small businesses. Education accounts for 56% of the total. The July increase came mainly from the “provision of other services” category, which added 61 companies. The latest rise follows an earlier increase in 2023, while the number of Nigerian companies declined in 2024 and 2025.

Sierra Leone sees 2.5-fold increase

Companies with Sierra Leonean founders increased from 30 on July 1 to 75 on Aug. 1. The 45 new registrations exceeded the total number recorded at the beginning of July.

The increase was concentrated in the “provision of other services” category, which went from zero to 44 companies. Education accounted for 20 organizations, up by one during the month.

World.title: South Ossetia residents name region’s main problems ahead of presidential election
World.content:
South Ossetia presidential election

South Ossetia election. Illustration created by Caucasian Knot using AI

A report by Caucasian Knot

Population decline, low wages, unemployment, queues at the customs checkpoint and poor public transport. Residents of South Ossetia named these as the main problems ahead of the snap presidential election.

Murad Valiev, Kazbek Kodoev, Marat Kambolov and Zurab Kokoev have been cleared to stand in the election. The Central Election Commission plans to print 40,000 ballot papers. Khokh Chochiev, leader of the Iry Farn party, who was denied registration, called the election a sham.

On 23 August, a Caucasian Knot correspondent spoke to residents of the region. The survey is not representative and reflects individual views.

“There is no trust left in anyone”

Fatima, 45, works as a kindergarten teacher in Tskhinval. She sees the lack of jobs as the main reason people are leaving the region.

“Young people mostly leave because of this. Graduates of Russian universities return home but cannot find work. If jobs become available here, they will come back,” she says.

Fatima also wants to see higher wages. She says incomes remain low while prices continue to rise. She also names queues at the customs checkpoint as another major problem.

“They said the situation improved after Kambolov visited the customs checkpoint. But there are still queues. I am not following the campaign. There is no trust left in anyone. I have not come across any campaigning either,” she said.

Karina, 23, is unemployed and lives in Dzau. She lists wages, unemployment, environmental problems and the state of agriculture among the region’s main challenges.

Public transport is a particular concern for her. The last bus leaves Dzau at 17:00, while the last bus from Tskhinval leaves at 18:00.

“I would like buses to run at least until eight or nine in the evening. I do not have a car and cannot afford to buy one. It is also practically impossible to get a loan or mortgage in South Ossetia,” Karina says.

In her view, unless these problems are addressed, the population decline will become irreversible.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions”

Karina is not following the election campaign and believes the outcome has already been decided.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions. They would benefit from making Kambolov president. The election is just window dressing. People have not had a choice for a long time,” she said.

Karina says she has not seen campaign posters or activists in Dzau or Tskhinval.

World.title: Why has Georgia’s government revived debate over Treaty of Georgievsk?
World.content:
In recent days, Georgian government officials have made a series of similar statements about the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the agreement with Russia saved Georgia and the Georgian nation. He argues that it laid the foundations for today’s sovereign state and helped preserve its European prospects.

Several days later, other leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party began speaking about the Treaty of Georgievsk in similar terms. They repeat not only the main conclusion but also the same arguments: Georgia faced the threat of destruction, an agreement with Russia was the only option, and that decision saved the Georgian nation, Christianity and Georgian statehood.

This level of coordination suggests that the discussion has moved beyond a spontaneous debate about history. The positive assessment of the Treaty of Georgievsk sounds more like a unified political message from Georgian Dream.

But what is the purpose of this message?

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement under which eastern Georgia (the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti) came under the protection of the Russian Empire. The parties signed the treaty in the summer of 1783 at the fortress of Georgievsk. The treaty protected Georgia from external threats but ultimately led to the complete loss of its independence.

Opposition figures say the government is preparing the public for a possible new agreement with Russia. Former president Mikheil Saakashvili, who is currently in prison, has even referred to specific draft agreements.

Other political commentators see the renewed focus on the treaty as an attempt to divert attention from important current issues. Against the backdrop of what they describe as the Georgian government’s increasingly pro-Russian course and anti-Western rhetoric, the Treaty of Georgievsk is a particularly sensitive issue for politically active Georgians and can easily provoke a strong reaction.

According to this view, the government deliberately sparked a historical debate to draw attention away from corruption within the administration. At the same time, the authorities have intensified the charges against former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili. His case goes beyond the actions of an individual official and raises questions about the scale of systemic corruption itself.

Russian media have already described Kobakhidze’s remarks as another sign that Tbilisi’s attitude towards Moscow is changing.

So why has a treaty signed 243 years ago suddenly become one of the main topics of Georgia’s current political debate?

What Prime Minister Kobakhidze said

Irakli Kobakhidze has made several statements about the Treaty of Georgievsk. His main argument is that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation.

On 18 August, Kobakhidze described the signing of the treaty as a “civilisational choice”. He said Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose fellow Orthodox Russia.

“The fact that today we are an independent, sovereign state based on traditional European values and traditional European culture is precisely the result of this pragmatic decision taken by Erekle II,” the prime minister said.

Kobakhidze has also argued that Erekle II’s decision was not only justified, but the “only correct and only possible” choice at the time. In his account, Russia honoured the terms of the agreement during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end. Almost 20 years passed between the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country was effectively saved.”

Kobakhidze presented Russia’s abolition of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti as a process that became possible only after the Georgian king’s death: “When Erekle II died, unfortunately, events took a different course.”

Georgian Dream leaders have also drawn parallels between this historical episode and modern Georgian-Russian relations.

Kobakhidze compared the Treaty of Georgievsk with the August 2008 war and said that “under Mikheil Saakashvili’s leadership, all the agreements, whether signed or unsigned, were torn up over our heads.”

Other party leaders have expressed similar views. MP David Matikashvili, for example, called the Treaty of Georgievsk a “smart and wise” decision.

“Ultimately, despite the many negative consequences, Georgia and the Georgian people managed to survive physically. The genius of King Erekle is obvious here,” he said.

More about the Treaty of Georgievsk

The Treaty of Georgievsk was signed in 1783 between the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. It was not an agreement between a united Georgia and Russia. At the time, the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia were not parties to the treaty.

Under the agreement, Kartli-Kakheti came under Russian protection. In return, Russia undertook to protect its territorial integrity and the Bagrationi dynasty.

Historian Beka Kobakhidze strongly disputes Kobakhidze’s claim that Russia honoured the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime. He writes that the period from 1783 until Erekle’s death was instead one of the most difficult periods of his reign.

In 1785, an army led by Avar ruler Omar Khan invaded Kartli-Kakheti. Beka Kobakhidze says Erekle had warned Russia about the planned attack and requested the assistance provided for under the treaty. Russia did not provide it.

Agha Mohammad Khan’s 1795 campaign had even more devastating consequences. After the Battle of Krtsanisi, his forces captured and looted Tbilisi. Thousands of people were killed or taken captive.

Beka Kobakhidze draws on these facts to write:

“Irakli Kobakhidze is falsifying history. The period from 1783 to 1798, from the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk to Erekle’s death, was the most difficult and destructive period of his reign.”

In 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. The Bagrationi royal family lost power, and some of its members were exiled to Russia. The Russian Empire later conquered and annexed the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia as well.

Was Georgia “on the brink of extinction”?

Another key element of Georgian Dream’s new historical narrative concerns demographic survival. The prime minister says the Georgian nation faced a “real threat of extinction” at the end of the 18th century. MP Matikashvili has also referred to the “physical survival” of the Georgian people.

This view is not new. The Russian imperial narrative, and later the Soviet version of history, often portrayed the annexation of Georgia as a painful but necessary step to save the country.

Historian Giorgi Ugulava wrote in a 2025 article for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that this representation was one of the main products of Russian imperial propaganda. The argument was that Georgia could not survive independently and that Russian protection was the best option available.

Why has Erekle II become a political symbol for Georgian Dream?

Georgian Dream’s political campaign around Erekle II began well before August 2026.

In 2023, literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili criticised Erekle II over the Treaty of Georgievsk. Georgian Dream leaders responded with fierce criticism of the scholar. That same year, the pro-Russian Conservative Movement disrupted one of Berdzenishvili’s lectures. He was later attacked in the street.

At the time, Georgian Dream chairman Irakli Kobakhidze said violence was unacceptable. At the same time, however, he accused Berdzenishvili of acting against Georgian identity.

In August 2024, Kobakhidze announced plans to erect a new monument to Erekle II in Tbilisi. The monument opened on 24 September 2025. At the ceremony, Kobakhidze described Erekle II as a symbol of “patriotism”, “love of the homeland” and “pragmatism”.

Kobakhidze also claimed that foreign diplomats had criticised Erekle II during meetings with Georgian Dream representatives. He did not name any of the diplomats or specify which countries they represented. However, according to his account, criticism of Erekle II formed part of coordinated actions by Western diplomats and the Georgian opposition.

Erekle II has therefore gradually evolved from a historical figure into a symbol of the current political confrontation. On one side stands the “pragmatic” king who reached an agreement with Russia. On the other are his critics, whom the government portrays as agents of Western interests.

“A new treaty”: what do pro-Russian forces in Georgia want?

While Georgian Dream highlights the positive historical significance of the old Treaty of Georgievsk, openly operating pro-Russian forces in Georgia are already calling directly for a “new treaty”.

One of the main figures in this campaign is Russian-Georgian citizen Mamuka Pipia, leader of the Solidarity for Peace party.

In July 2025, Pipia called for the signing of a “Treaty of Georgievsk 2” and an alliance treaty with Russia. His proposals included restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and removing Article 78 from Georgia’s Constitution. The article requires constitutional bodies to take all measures to ensure Georgia’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Pipia said: “Given today’s geopolitical situation, Russia and Georgia need to support each other, and they need to formalise an alliance treaty on equal terms.”

In August 2026, Pipia described Kobakhidze’s statements as a success for his own political agenda.

“I am glad that the country’s leadership now recognises the reality that we have been speaking about openly for the past two years,” he said.

Pipia says his idea of a “new Treaty of Georgievsk” means “a completely new, comprehensive and, most importantly, equal treaty with the Russian Federation”.

“We are working in this direction, and Moscow will make an appropriate statement very soon,” he added.

Georgian Dream denies coordinating with pro-Russian groups. However, Pipia’s political network maintains open contacts with Russian officials. He has appeared in public at various times with Russian State Duma deputies and other senior Russian officials.

In May 2025, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who is under US sanctions, was also in Red Square with Pipia. The US Treasury Department has described Partskhaladze as a Georgian-Russian oligarch and said Russia’s FSB used him to influence Georgian society and politics.

How closely do the two narratives align?

Mamuka Pipia’s and Georgian Dream’s ultimate political demands do not currently coincide. Georgian Dream is not officially calling for an alliance treaty with Russia, a “new treaty” or the repeal of Article 78 of the Constitution. This is a significant difference.

However, the similarities in their rhetoric are clear. In both cases, the main arguments for closer relations with Russia are “pragmatism”, peace, security and national interests. In both narratives, the West is increasingly portrayed not as a security partner but as a source of threats or pressure.

The rhetoric around the “deep state” also overlaps. For years, Pipia has spoken about Western forces allegedly trying to use Georgia against Russia. A similar conspiracy theory has become part of Georgian Dream’s official political messaging in recent years.

Now another important element has entered this shared vocabulary: the interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk as an agreement that saved Georgia.

What does the opposition say about a possible new agreement?

Against this backdrop, Georgian opposition figures suspect that the historical debate may serve to prepare public opinion for a more concrete political decision.

Mikheil Saakashvili said that the government was carrying out “ideological preparations for signing a treaty of betrayal”. He claims that Russia has even given ruling-party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili drafts of several agreements.

Saakashvili referred to restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and separate agreements on Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. He also claims that Irakli Kobakhidze is expected to travel to Moscow in the coming weeks.

There is currently no independent confirmation of this information. Neither the Georgian nor the Russian authorities have officially announced preparations for such agreements.

Former diplomat Ghia Japaridze also sees the government’s rhetoric as preparation for possible changes in foreign policy. He says the government is using the Treaty of Georgievsk to “justify a change in Georgia’s foreign policy course”.

What is the Russian media saying?

Irakli Kobakhidze’s statements have also attracted attention in Russia.

On 21 August, the Russian publication Vzglyad published an article headlined “Georgia has taken an important step towards normality”.

The article links several issues: the Georgian government’s campaign against so-called “Russophobia”, accusations against the West and the new interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk.

The publication places particular emphasis on the “restoration of respect for the Treaty of Georgievsk — an alliance with Russia that saved Georgia”.

In other words, what Georgian officials present in Tbilisi as a historical interpretation and an assessment of Erekle II’s decision is already being read by Russian media as a sign of changing political attitudes towards modern Russia.

A day earlier, even more far-reaching claims circulated in Russian Telegram channels. INSIDER-T, citing unofficial sources, claimed that Tbilisi had offered Moscow a behind-the-scenes deal: “full geopolitical loyalty” from Georgia in exchange for Russia publicly abandoning the annexation of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

These claims are also not supported by reliable evidence.

What matters, however, is the political expectations now emerging in the Russian information space in response to statements by Georgian officials.

A historical dispute or an ongoing political process?

There is currently no publicly confirmed evidence that the Georgian authorities are preparing to sign a “New Treaty of Georgievsk” or another alliance agreement with Russia.

However, it is difficult to describe what is happening as merely a dispute among historians.

On one side is a government that has sharply worsened relations with Georgia’s main Western partners in recent years and has effectively frozen the country’s EU accession process.

On the other are pro-Russian groups openly calling for a political alliance and security ties with Russia. They see the prime minister’s new rhetoric as a victory for their position.

This is accompanied by the reaction of the Russian information space, where Georgian government statements are increasingly seen as a sign that Tbilisi is turning towards the Kremlin.

Against this backdrop, the significance of the Treaty of Georgievsk is no longer confined to the 18th century. The key question now is why the government needs to convince the public that a historical agreement with Russia, which ultimately led to the annexation of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, saved Georgia.

And, more importantly, what modern political choice might this version of history be intended to justify?

Debate over the Treaty of Georgievsk in Georgia

World.title: 750,000 lari bribe and other new allegations against jailed former Georgian PM who turned against the government
World.content:
Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

Former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili

New charges have been brought against former Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili for accepting a large bribe. The charges came shortly after he published open letters accusing the government of persecuting him to prevent his return to politics.

Garibashvili is already serving a five-year sentence for legalising illicit income. The new charges carry a prison sentence of between 11 and 15 years.

🟥 According to the prosecution, then-defence minister Juansher Burchuladze, who is now in prison, illegally transferred 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Garibashvili in cash in several instalments.

What does the prosecution accuse Garibashvili of?

The case concerns the purchase of medical equipment and supplies for the Defence Ministry. According to the prosecution, the ministry conducted three secret procurement procedures from late 2022 onwards.

At the time, Juansher Burchuladze served as defence minister, while Irakli Garibashvili was prime minister.

According to investigators, Burchuladze and his relative, Vasil Mcheidze, reached an agreement with a local business and offered it an opportunity to take part in government tenders. With their help, the business was supposed to win the tenders and then pay them 10% of the total contract value.

The businessman demanded additional guarantees.

According to the prosecution, Burchuladze then reached an agreement with Irakli Garibashvili, who was serving as prime minister.

Investigators accuse the former prime minister of protecting the scheme and demanding his share of the proceeds.

According to the indictment, deputy defence minister Giorgi Khaindrava and procurement department head Vladimir Gudushauri then created non-competitive conditions. This allowed selected companies to win the tenders at predetermined prices.

The prosecution says the companies supplied the ministry with goods worth 18,484,960 lari (about $7.5 million). However, the actual value of the goods was 11,499,705 lari (about $4.5 million).

The prosecution estimates the damage to the state at 6,985,255 lari (about $2.6 million).

How was the 1.9 million lari divided?

According to the investigation, the businessman ultimately transferred 1.9 million lari (about $730,000) to Vasil Mcheidze in several instalments. The amount represented roughly 10% of the total value of the contracts.

Vasil Mcheidze kept 400,000 lari (about $155,000);

he transferred 1.5 million lari (about $580,000) to Juansher Burchuladze;

Burchuladze kept 750,000 lari (about $290,000);

he transferred the remaining 750,000 lari (about $290,000) to Irakli Garibashvili.

Prosecutors have charged the former prime minister under Article 338 of the Criminal Code. The article covers accepting a particularly large bribe by a public or political official as part of a group.

At this stage, the prosecution is asking the court to schedule a preliminary hearing. It is not seeking a new pre-trial measure because Garibashvili is already in custody.

Who gave investigators new testimony?

According to the prosecution, Vasil Mcheidze decided to cooperate with investigators on 12 August. He provided the authorities with information in his possession.

Juansher Burchuladze is also cooperating with the investigation. The prosecution is relying on their testimony to establish Garibashvili’s role in the new case.

Burchuladze was arrested in September 2025. On 23 April 2026, a court sentenced him to 10 years in prison for abuse of power and legalising illicit income.

Burchuladze’s former deputy, Giorgi Khaindrava, and Vasil Mcheidze each received eight-year prison sentences in the same case. Gudushauri reached a plea agreement with the prosecution.

Why does the timing of the new charges against Garibashvili matter?

Just days before prosecutors brought the new charges, Garibashvili made three statements from prison. They were published on 17, 18 and 20 August.

The former prime minister said the ruling party was demanding that he admit to additional acts of corruption. He said the government feared his return to politics.

Garibashvili also said he had received a letter from prominent Georgian Dream representative Mamuka Mdinaradze. According to Garibashvili, a close friend of Mdinaradze delivered the letter to a member of his family.

“You sent me to prison for five years because of false assumptions, fantasies, envy, fears and suspicions created by a certain group within the party,” Garibashvili wrote.

He said the demand that he admit to the new allegations came with a hint that authorities could arrest his father.

“I am not fighting anyone. I am only defending myself and my family. That is why I will have no choice but to respond in kind to everything you do,” Garibashvili said.

The new charges have given the former prime minister’s statements added significance. However, his account has not been investigated or independently verified.

What does Georgian Dream say?

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze suggested that Garibashvili may have had information about the ongoing investigation. In his view, the former prime minister’s statements were pre-emptive.

“Former politicians often use this method, and legal issues are sometimes brought into the political sphere,” Kaladze said.

He said Garibashvili’s safety and rights were protected.

Mamuka Mdinaradze denies Garibashvili’s allegations. He considers the current case against the former prime minister part of the government’s fight against corruption.

Garibashvili family’s response

Garibashvili’s wife’s brother, Alexander Tamazashvili, published an extract from the public registry after prosecutors brought the new charges. He said the document showed a property transaction involving Zurab Tukvadze, a businessman and one of the prosecution’s witnesses.

The prosecution’s public statement does not name the businessman. However, Tamazashvili claims that Tukvadze transferred a country house in the Tskneti settlement to Vasil Mcheidze in 2023. Tamazashvili suggested that the property transfer amounted to a bribe.

The statement can also be seen as an ironic rebuttal of the allegations. However, the published property transaction neither proves nor disproves that anyone may have given cash to Garibashvili.

Garibashvili himself has not publicly responded to the details of the new charges.

Opposition raises two possible concerns

Opposition representatives have highlighted two issues in the case.

The first is possible corruption in defence procurement.

The second is the suspicion that the law may serve as a tool of political pressure.

Levan Samushia, a member of the opposition Strong Georgia – Lelo party, said Garibashvili’s earlier statements give grounds for such suspicions.

“Is the law not being used in this case to exert pressure based on clan interests? Otherwise, how could Garibashvili have known in advance that he might face charges?” Samushia said.

Zurab Japaridze, leader of Girchi – More Freedom, drew attention to the scheme described in the indictment. He linked Garibashvili’s alleged receipt of cash to his previous case.

“He artificially inflated the price, received his share in cash in lari, then exchanged it for dollars and gold and kept the bundles in a safe,” Japaridze wrote.

Garibashvili’s first case

Garibashvili first faced corruption charges in October 2025. Investigators accused him of legalising a particularly large amount of illicit income.

According to the prosecution, Garibashvili provided false information in his property declarations. In doing so, he allegedly attempted to give illegally obtained income a legitimate appearance.

In January 2026, Garibashvili pleaded guilty and reached a deal with the prosecution. The court sentenced him to five years in prison.

Garibashvili has not pleaded guilty in the new case. The main grounds for the charges are testimony from Burchuladze and Mcheidze. The court will have to assess the credibility of their statements, along with the other evidence.

The case now brings together two parallel questions.

One concerns possible corruption in secret Defence Ministry procurement procedures.

The other concerns Garibashvili’s claim that the government demanded that he admit guilt in advance.

Charges against former Georgian Prime Minister Garibashvili

World.title: $12m dispute and house sold at auction: where has former Georgian PM Nika Gilauri gone? – RFE/RL
World.content:
Nika Gilauri case

At the end of 2024, former prime minister Nika Gilauri became one of the most vocal critics of the ruling Georgian Dream party. Over the following months, he faced serious problems: authorities seized his foundation, while a court ordered him and his companies to pay $12 million in compensation to former business partners. Gilauri himself stopped appearing in public.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty published an investigation into the case. The circumstances described in the report raise suspicions that the legal proceedings against Gilauri may amount to political persecution. Georgian and German lawyers have called the court ruling unfounded.

The material draws on a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty investigation.

Gilauri’s house put up for forced auction

On 16 July 2026, the National Bureau of Enforcement put Nika Gilauri’s house in Tsavkisi up for auction. A 3,368-square-metre plot of land and a 1,157-square-metre villa sold for almost four million lari (about $1.54 million).

The property had an estimated value of 4.876 million lari (about $1.87 million), but bidding started at 10% of that amount. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, businessman Vano Sturua bought the house. He is a former business partner of Nika Gilauri’s brother, Irakli.

Since 2018, this house has remained the only property in Georgia registered in Gilauri’s name. However, court rulings have also ordered the seizure of other assets and his shares in companies.

Gilauri himself has not commented on the situation. He only responded to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty in writing:

“The legal proceedings are still ongoing, and on my lawyers’ advice, I will not make any comments or give interviews at this stage.”

Gilauri’s return to politics

Nika Gilauri served as energy minister and finance minister under Mikheil Saakashvili. He then headed the government from 2009 to 2012. After leaving public service, he founded the consulting company Reformatics and stayed out of Georgia’s public political life for about 12 years.

The situation changed ahead of the 2024 parliamentary election. A few days before the vote, Gilauri and the Reformatics team presented a 100-page document outlining their vision for a “Third Republic of Georgia”. It addressed Georgia’s exit from Russia’s sphere of influence, judicial independence and European integration.

Media reports said Gilauri was financing the opposition Coalition for Change. Several coalition leaders later confirmed that they had worked with him and received campaign donations.

After security forces violently dispersed protests in November and December 2024, Gilauri called the Georgian Dream government illegitimate. He demanded new elections and the release of detained protesters.

Gilauri also called on business representatives to create a fund to support protesters. His Prosperity foundation raised 246,000 lari (about $94,450) in three months. The money was intended to support protesters and people who had lost their jobs because of their political views.

In March 2025, the prosecutor’s office froze the assets of the Prosperity foundation and four other foundations. Authorities opened an investigation into allegations of sabotage, assisting the activities of a hostile foreign organisation and actions against the constitutional order. The investigation remains ongoing, and the foundations remain suspended.

Gilauri has not appeared in public since then.

Dispute over the construction of three hydropower plants

The multimillion-lari legal dispute involving Gilauri began several years before he returned to politics.

In 2015, Aquahydro signed memorandums with the Georgian government and state-owned companies to build three small hydropower plants in the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region: Ipari, Khelra and Nakra.

Black Sea Group took responsibility for the construction work. Under the agreement, the contractor would receive payment for the completed work as well as a 20% stake in the company operating the hydropower plants.

Ipari and Khelra were completed and brought into operation. However, Black Sea Group halted construction of Nakra in 2020. A few months later, Aquahydro terminated its contract with the company and hired another contractor to complete the project.

In 2021, Black Sea Group went to court. The company said it had not received full payment for the work it had completed. It sought several million lari in compensation, as well as damages for lost profits.

Gilauri’s side filed a counterclaim seeking 14.5 million lari (about $5.57 million) from Black Sea Group. They argued that the suspension of construction at Nakra deprived the company of expected revenue for 2020-2022. Their expert assessment found that the contractor had received $600,000 more than the actual cost of the work, according to official documentation.

Black Sea Group rejected the assessment, arguing that it had not received full payment for the work it had completed.

Why was Gilauri held personally liable?

On 12 February 2025, Tbilisi City Court judge Liana Kajashvili ruled in favour of Black Sea Group. The court ordered the former prime minister and companies under his control to pay Black Sea Group more than $12 million in damages.

The Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court upheld the ruling. It became final in November 2025. The amount owed continues to increase each day until the court order is enforced.

The direct parties to the dispute were Aquahydro and Black Sea Group. Nika Gilauri had no direct contractual relationship with either company. He owned a stake in a firm whose subsidiary acted as the project’s direct client.

Despite this corporate structure, the court held Gilauri personally liable. It also imposed liability on Reformatics, even though the company had no involvement in the hydropower project.

The court concluded that Gilauri and companies linked to him had acted together against Black Sea Group under what it described as a “joint agreement”.

What do the lawyers say?

German and Georgian lawyers Heinz Böling and Giorgi Jughéli analysed the ruling. Their analysis appeared in a German legal journal in June 2026.

The authors argue that the court conflated the common goal of the economic project with the legal liability of the individual companies involved. They believe the ruling effectively erases the distinction between a company and its partners.

“Neither German nor Georgian law provides for such legal consequences. This is incorrect and, moreover, as already stated, simply fabricated,” the lawyers write.

In their assessment, the court imposed personal liability “through three corporate veils” on a person who was not a party to the disputed contract.

“As far as we know, there is no other court ruling allowing such liability — not only in Georgia, but anywhere in the world,” the authors note.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty also asked two other Georgian lawyers to independently review the ruling. Both said there were insufficient legal grounds for holding Gilauri and Reformatics liable.

One of the lawyers said that common ownership does not automatically make companies liable for each other’s obligations. To impose personal liability, the court would have had to prove that Gilauri used the corporate structure to defraud a creditor or pursue other unlawful purposes. The ruling contains no such evidence or reasoning.

There is no documented evidence of a political link between Gilauri’s public criticism, the acceleration of the court proceedings and the final ruling. However, the chronology raises questions. The trial court concluded a four-year dispute about two months after Gilauri made a series of high-profile political statements. The higher courts then reviewed the extensive case file within eight months.

The state has now sold Gilauri’s house at auction. The former prime minister remains silent, while authorities continue to pursue his assets and business interests to recover the money.

Nika Gilauri case

World.title: Aliyev’s Uzbekistan visit: ‘Eternal friendship’ and family business expansion
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Uzbekistan

The state visit to Tashkent was presented by official media as a “new, symbolic and practical stage” in relations between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev held a one-on-one meeting, chaired the third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council, signed a “Treaty on Eternal Friendship”, awarded each other their countries’ highest state honours, and took part in ceremonies marking the opening and laying of foundations for Azerbaijani investment projects in Uzbekistan.

However, behind the official statements and rhetoric about “brotherhood” lie specific financial and business interests. Against the backdrop of the visit, attention has also focused on the parallel expansion of private companies directly or indirectly linked to Ilham Aliyev’s family, including PASHA Holding and Emin Agalarov’s Sea Breeze project.

What happened?

The main document signed during the visit was the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship”. Under the treaty, the two sides intend to build relations based on the principles of eternal friendship, mutual trust, strategic partnership and alliance, as well as support each other’s national development models. They undertake not to join blocs or alliances that could harm the other side’s sovereignty, security or territorial integrity, and not to allow their territory to be used by third parties for such purposes or for the activities of such groups.

Areas of cooperation outlined in the treaty include strengthening the UN’s central role, developing interparliamentary ties, trade and investment, including in energy, transport and logistics, digital development, agriculture, the green and digital economies, e-commerce, ICT and space technologies. The treaty also provides for the development of interconnected transport systems, the preservation of cultural and humanitarian ties, language learning, scientific and educational exchanges, interregional cooperation and tourism.

The heads of state exchanged their countries’ highest state honours, with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev receiving the Heydar Aliyev Order. Ceremonies were also held to open and lay the foundations for specific Azerbaijani projects in Uzbekistan, including hotel and residential complexes, tourism facilities, a building for the Nizami Ganjavi University, an “Azerbaijan” park and other facilities.

Joint projects have been launched in banking and finance, construction materials production, education, the oil and gas sector, tourism, housing construction, mining and agriculture. A corresponding “road map” was also adopted.

Azerbaijan’s state-owned bank enters Uzbek market

President Ilham Aliyev cited several specific examples of cooperation, including the entry of a leading Azerbaijani bank into the Uzbek market, the expansion of SOCAR’s retail network, oil and gas exploration nearing its final stage, and the prospect of drilling production wells next year.

The bank in question is the International Bank of Azerbaijan (ABB), the country’s largest state-owned bank, with around 88–92% of its shares held by the Finance Ministry and other state bodies. ABB is acquiring a 51% controlling stake in the privately owned Uzbek bank Davr Bank, investing more than $100m in the deal.

Despite its state-owned status, ABB was previously implicated in the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal, involving a $2.9bn money-laundering scheme. The bank is now entering the Uzbek market with the backing of state resources and political will. The deal is being presented as a purely commercial decision, but comes against the backdrop of a strengthening political alliance between the two countries.

Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov announced the deal at an interregional forum a day before the visit, and it was formally concluded on the day of the visit. ABB will operate in Uzbekistan under the Davr Bank brand. The bank has assets of around $1bn, a customer base of 1.4 million and a network of 43 branches. Fitch Ratings expects the deal to be completed by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Expansion of businesses linked to Aliyev family

Alongside the official banking deal, several private projects have also attracted attention during the visit and in the preceding period. Some are linked to companies and structures directly or indirectly associated with the president’s family.

Sea Breeze Uzbekistan: A $5bn resort project being developed by Agalarov Development, owned by Emin Agalarov, the former husband of President Aliyev’s daughter Leyla Aliyeva. The complex is planned for a 577-hectare site on the shores of the Charvak Reservoir. In 2025, the project was presented directly to Mirziyoyev and fast-tracked without a tender, while the environmental assessment had not yet been fully completed. A foundation-laying ceremony took place on the day of the visit. Although Agalarov is no longer related to the presidential family by marriage, he continues to enjoy high-level political support.

The complex is planned for a 577-hectare site on the shores of the Charvak Reservoir. In 2025, the project was presented directly to Mirziyoyev and fast-tracked without a tender, while the environmental assessment had not yet been fully completed. A foundation-laying ceremony took place on the day of the visit. Although Agalarov is no longer related to the presidential family by marriage, he continues to enjoy high-level political support. PASHA Holding projects: The holding company, which has been linked to the president’s daughters Leyla and Arzu Aliyeva, as well as to Mehriban Aliyeva’s father Arif Pashayev, is building a Ritz-Carlton-branded hotel and residential complex in Tashkent. The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates.

The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Kazakhstan strengthens Caspian Sea emergency fleet with new vessel
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. A delegation from Kazakhstan's Ministry of Emergency Situations, together with Tengiz Zhasagy, has completed the acceptance of a new DAMEN Fast Crew Supplier 2710 vessel.

This was announced by the press service of the Ministry of Emergency Situations.

Built by DAMEN Workboats at its production facility in Kuressaare, Estonia, the vessel is designed for search-and-rescue and emergency response operations, oil spill response, rapid intervention during emergencies, and ensuring navigational safety in Kazakhstan's sector of the Caspian Sea.

The vessel's arrival comes as the Caspian Sea continues to experience declining water levels and increasingly shallow conditions in some areas. Changes in navigation conditions increase the risk of vessels running aground and other incidents that could threaten lives and cause environmental damage.

"The new vessel will allow Kazakhstan's rescuers to reach the scene of an incident faster, provide timely assistance to people in distress and respond more effectively to the consequences of accidents," the ministry said.

The DAMEN Fast Crew Supplier 2710 is expected to strengthen the operational capabilities of Kazakhstan's emergency fleet, enabling faster response to maritime incidents and supporting search-and-rescue and environmental protection operations.

World.title: Uzbekistan marks its 35th Independence anniversary with 163 new projects
World.content:
Photo: The Press service of the President of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. As part of the celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of independence, Uzbekistan has commissioned 72 major industrial and service facilities, as well as 91 social infrastructure projects across the country.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president.

According to the statement, Mirziyoyev took part in a ceremony marking the commissioning of new facilities and stated that over the past decade, Uzbekistan has laid the foundation for what he called a new era of national development.

Furthermore, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev emphasized that investment, industrial diversification, and job creation are key factors in the country’s economic transformation.

“The last 10 years will forever be written into the history of our country as a period of laying the foundation for a new era of revival — the Third Renaissance,” Mirziyoyev said.

According to the president, Uzbekistan’s economy has grown more than 2.5 times over the past decade, while the country has attracted $160 billion in foreign investment and commissioned 2,163 major industrial facilities worth a combined $76 billion. Nearly 6 million permanent jobs have been created during the period.

Mirziyoyev stated that the country was moving away from an economy dependent on raw-material exports toward one focused on deeper processing and higher-value products.

“We are moving from a country oriented toward exporting raw materials to an economy capable of bringing finished products to global markets through deep-processing value chains,” he said.

The projects commissioned Tuesday have a combined value of nearly 50 trillion soums (about $4.2 billion) and are expected to create 15,000 jobs and generate an additional 1 trillion soums (around $84.9 million) in annual budget revenues.

The new facilities span energy, agriculture, food processing, metallurgy, automotive manufacturing, electrical equipment, construction materials, mining and textiles.

Energy projects include 1,573 megawatts of new generating capacity in Syrdarya region, a 200-MW wind farm and 100-MW energy storage system in Karakalpakstan, and renewable facilities in Navoi region expected to generate 657 million kilowatt-hours annually.

The ceremony also highlighted major investments in education and healthcare. Among the 91 social facilities are 36 kindergartens, 43 schools, seven higher education institutions and three hospitals.

The new University of New Uzbekistan complex in Tashkent covers 10 hectares and can accommodate 7,000 students. A National Library with 30,000 square meters of space was also commissioned.

Mirziyoyev stressed that the value of the projects should not be measured solely by investment and export figures.

“Every investment you make strengthens the foundation of Uzbekistan’s future. Every job you create contributes to the well-being of families,” he said.

The president officially commissioned the projects by pressing a symbolic button at the end of the ceremony.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Mongolia explore regional connectivity via CKU railway
World.content:
Photo: the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Uzbekistan and Mongolia are exploring opportunities to expand trade and transportation ties through the “China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan” railway, which could open up new opportunities for strengthening ties with Central Asia and the South Caucasus.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, following a meeting between officials of the Ministry of Investment and Dulguun Damdin-Od, executive director of the International Think Tank for Landlocked Developing Countries.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, the sides reviewed prospects for expanding trade, economic, transport and logistics cooperation between the two countries. Bilateral trade reached $51.8 million in 2025, while a business forum held in May brought together more than 70 companies from Uzbekistan and Mongolia.

Particular attention was given to developing high value-added production, building resilient supply chains, opening new international transport routes, simplifying trade procedures and expanding the digitalization of cross-border processes.

The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway was highlighted as a potential driver of greater regional connectivity. Once implemented, the project could provide Mongolia with additional intermodal transport options linking its markets with Uzbekistan, other Central Asian countries and the South Caucasus.

“The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway can create additional opportunities for Mongolia to develop intermodal transport links with Uzbekistan and broader regional markets,” the sides noted during the meeting.

The discussions reflect efforts by the two landlocked countries to diversify trade routes and improve connectivity amid growing interest in regional transport corridors.

The sides also agreed to cooperate in preparing for and organizing the 25th CAREC Ministerial Conference, scheduled to take place in Ulaanbaatar in October.

The conference is expected to provide another platform for Uzbekistan and Mongolia to advance discussions on trade facilitation, regional connectivity and transport cooperation.
